THE CUCKOO.

A cuckoo by a small bird chased • Through openings in the forest green: That's what I saw as past they raced, A sight that's worthy to be seen. The cuckoo tried an egg to hide By stealth in its pursuer's nest; But quickly spied, was driven aside. In ignominious Ilight,hard pressed. What makes the smaller bold and strong, 'Yet fills the largeir bird with dread? The difference of right and wrong. The body's governed by the hPad ! LIEUT.-COLONEL FIFE COOKSON..

A Member of Parliament, well known for his ready and unfailing humour, had lately to undergo a serious operation in the leg. It was at one time feared that amputation would be necessary. Just as the operation was about to begin, the honourable member quietly re- marked to the surgeon, "Remember, that if you cut off my leg I can't stand for the boroafsh any mere. But," he added, after a pause, as if for cofaiideration, "after all, I shall be able to stump the country." TAICH A RAIN-BATIL—One of the best ways of refresh- ing the complexion is to expose it freely to the rain. A long walk, with the soft rain playing on c..ne's face, is a thorough beautifier, which umbrellas have robbed us of long enough. Equipped in waterproof cloak and cap of storm serge, leaving the face quite bare, one should walk hours at least to get the full benefit of the rain. Not only the rain but the vapour-laden air soaks the tissues, washing the skin more thoroughly than a Turkish bath, filling out the shrunken akin, parched by house heat and . .

obliterating fine wrinkles. Sleep and walking in the rain are two great aids to beauty, which preserved the charms of Diana of Poitiers, who never allowed weather to keep her indoors, and who never lost an umbrella, because she never had one. My Lord President of the Council being advanced to the Great Seal, said to Gondamar he formerly had a desire, and the same continued with him still, to lead a private life. So he were rid of the burden, he would very willingly forbear the honour. Gondamar would tell him a tale of an old rat that would needs leave the world, and acquainted the young rats that he would retire into his hole and spend his days solitary, and would enjoy no more comfort He commanded them not to offer to come in unto him. After three days, one rat, more hardy than the rest, incited some of his fel- lows to go with him to see how his father did; for he might be dead. They went in, and found the old rat sitting in the midst of a rich Parmesan cneese! So he applied the fable after his witty manner. THE QUAKER IN THE LANE.—In certain people patience has accomplished its perfect work. "Why she was such a patient woman," said a son, eulogising his mother, "that she'd let me eat eighteen hot pancakes as she fried 'em, and then go and mix another batch!" Whether such long suffering is altogether to be desired would probably be disputed by the dyspeptic. A Quaker one day driving through a narrow lane met a young man, who was also driving. There was not room enough for them to pass each other unless one should turn back to a point where the lane was broader. "I won't make room for you!" cried the young man. "See if I do!" "I think lam older than thou," said the Quaker. "I have a right to expect thee to turn about" "Well I won't !" resumed the other; and pulling out a news- paper he began reading. The Quaker settled back in his chair, and placidly contemplated the landscape. "Friend," said he finally, "when thou hest read that paper I should be glad if thou wouldst lend it to me." This calm assumption of ability to wait indefinitely was too much for the young man, and he yielded his point. THE REVENGE OF TlME.—Father: " How's this, Eleanor—a £5 bill rendered from Fuss and Feather ?" Daughter: "Oh, yes, papa, dear; that is for my Easter bonnet, you know. It was lovely. too." Father (grimly): "It ought to have been." Daughter "It was, I can assure you. Jack thought it a perfect gem." Father " Hem ! That was very kind of Jack." Daughter: 4' Yes, wasn't it? I don't mind letting you, papa, dear, see a bit of poetry he wrote about it on the fly-leaf of my album." Father (reading) : A flutter of ribbon, a fringe of lace, A bunch of posies nodding upon It; , Two tender eyes, a mignon face— This is my love in her Easter b.nnet. "Thanks, my dear. I appreciate your confidence and Jack's rhyme. I will not forget either."—One Year , Later.—Jack: "Eleanor, isn't £5 a big price for a spring bonnet?" Eleanor: "Oh, no, not specially; it was my Easter bonnet, you know." "Alt! I was not aware that milliners had Easter offerings too." Eleanor (pout- ing): "You know very well they do not. I meant that the bonnet was of superior design and elegance. Papa met me and said I had never looked prettier. Oh, and he sent a message to you too!" Jack: "What was that?" Eleanor: "He bade me be sure to tell you that my bonnet was very becoming, and that if you intended to write an ode to it as usual this year, he would suggest that you write in blank verse and affix your auto- graph.' Jack (reddening a little): "Your papa, Eleanor, is a very funny old gentleman."

The ladies of Bermuda have started a rifle club, of which the Governor's wife is president. They have a range of their own, where they practise at 100 yards with 200-calibre weapons, and are said to make remarkably good scores. There lare seventy members, and their first championship competition is to take place next month.

Dr. J. D. Morel!, the Glasgow grammarian, of whose "Analysis of Sentences" fifty-six thousand copies have been sold, and from which he draws a handsome royalty, is seventy-three years of age, an earnest Gladstonian, a pleasant, genial,accoriaplished man, a good linguist, and an excellent performer on several musical instruments.

Lady Butler will send in her picture to the Aca- demy, but will not stay for: .the exhibition, as she leaves almost immediately to join Sir William Butler at Alexandria. Lady Butler's subject is an Irish eviction, treated principally as a landscape under characteristic conditions of climate, though the dramatic interest centres in a tragic female figure.

The Queen was looking very well again lastweek, though not quite so pleasant as at. the previous Drawing-room. She did not stay all the time, so that many missed seeing her. She sat a good deal, for she cannot now stand very long or go upstairs, and on the occasion of her visits to Lady Ely and the Duchess of Fife she was received on both occa- sions downstairs.

The rheumatism from which her 'Majesty is suffering, which has become chronic since her fall, has caused a contraction of the muscles of the leg. It does not impair her general health, as she is and looks well, but there is na disguising the fact, which every one admits who sees her, that the Queen has aged much in the last two years.

The postmen have taken a wise step. A deputa- tion of them yesterday interviewed a few of the M.P.'s most interested in the labor question, and got a promise that their grievances shall be laid before the House. The " grievances " include (1) freedom to "meet, disease, and combine"; (2) improved wages; (3) regular hours; (4) the abolition of pay- ment by the system of grading.

One of the attractions in St. Petersburg society this season is an immense Eiffel Tower one hundred and sixty feet high, composed of ten thousand blocks of crystal ice. On the first " platform "is a restaur- ant, yvhere everything is served cold, and which forms the favourite rendezvous of fashionable St. Petersburg. At night the tower is brilliantly illumi- nated with electric light forming a striking fea- ture.

The newest evening shoes are braided with very narrow strips of kid, the colour of the dress with which they are worn. The strips are put on about the eighth of an ineh apart, and arti so applied that the most serviceable and amply proportioned feet look well in them. The neatest looking are of white kid braided with black. Black with red stripes also look well, but the white foundation shows up the braiding most effectively.

Every summer thousands of visitors make pil- grimages to the cottage in which Robert Burns was born, near Alloway Kirk and the banks o' Doon. They are shown the room in which the poet first saw the light, as well as the " original " furniture used by Burn's parents. Will it be believed that all the genuinely original furniture of the cottage was sold off by public roup in September, 1843, most of it being risrw in the possession of a gentleman in Man- chester, who wants a thousand pounds for it.

The Lincolnshire rat plague, despite an enormous destruction of the vermin during the past few months, still continues. One farmer near Boston scatters poisoned barley about his yard at night, and gathers a huge crop of dead rats on the following morning. One day last week no fewer, it is stated, than 1,300 were counted,3oo another day,and smaller numbers since. Many farmers in the district are now adopting the same method/ In Billingboro' Fen 300 rats were killed from one stack during thrashing operations on Friday.

Country gentlemen will be interested to learn that the Hares Preservation Bill has come down from the Lords, and has been read a second time in the House of Commons. The bill provides a closed time for hares, and inflicts a penalty, not exceed- ing one pound, on any person who shall wilfully kill, wound, or take any bare or leveret, or use any gun, net, snare, or dog, for the purpose of killing, wounding, or taking any hare or leveret; or shall have in his possession any hare or leveret killed, wounded, or taken between the 15th day of March and the Ist day of. July.

The designs for the now Towerof London, which, under the auspices of Sir Edward Watkin and Com- pany, is going to far exceed the structure erected in Paris by M. Eiffel, have all been handed in. They are nearly two hundred in number, and many of them, it is said, are of great beauty and engineering merit. The jurors, of whom Sir Frederick Bram- well is the chairman, met on Saturday last, and set aside seventy of the best designs for further con- sideration. The first prize is 500 guineas, and the second 250 guineas, and all the designs will be pub- licly exhibited.

The wearing of the shamrock was very conspicu- ous in the House on Monday night. English Liberals wore the emblem as well as Irish Nationalists, as has been the custom of late years. The one curious exception Was that the Orangemen dropped the custom to which they had previously adhered and failed to sport the trefoil. Why they did this no one quite knew. The shamrock is not a party or even a Catholic emblem, and on St. Patrick's Day all the Irish regiments, and Irishmen, without distinc- tion of creed or politics, delight to show it. The action of the Orangemen is only another ptoof that these gentlemen grow narrower fanatics as they grow older.

The passion for research takes many forms, but few more curious than that to which "The Chemist aud Druggist" devoted itself when it asked its subscribers throughout the United Kingdom to supply it with estimates of the number of pills con- sumed in the United Kingdom daily. The investi- gation should establish our renown as a pill-taking nation, for the extraordinary number of 6,643,961

pills is computed to he the daily consumption. This would give one pill per week to every man, woman, and child in the kingdom. loascinatea with its own calculations, "The Chemist and Druggist" goes on to show that, taking the average pill to weigh three grains, a year's supply for the 13nited 'Kingdom would weigh not less than 178 tons, or sufficient to 1111 thirty-six ordinary railway wagons. Moreover, if the pills were placed in a row, the distance covered would be as great as from Lifierpool to New York and back again.

If ever a political prophet was justified by events, Lord Randolph Churchill is that prophet. His famous memorandum warned the Government (1) that the Commissioners theinselves, whatever their verdict, must become the "object of political criticism and animadversion," and that no judge could emerge from the inquiry with the same moral weight and influence as when he went into it; (2) that the tribunal would conduct its proceedings by methods unknown to courts of law, and that the evidence extracted might be used for other pur- poses ; (3) that whatever its decision the House of Commons would still have to deal with the Irish members; (4) that a decision adverse to the "limes" would result in proceedings for libel in which that paper would be at a great disadvantage, and so on Almost every item of the prophecy has been fulfilled' Nevertheless, Lord Randolph's Executive net on Monday night to censure him. The prophet, as i usual, s without honour in his own country.

' " The 'Poet for all time' "—writes a correspondent (R. C. R., Hampstead)—" must surely have had a prophetic inkling of the Parnell Commission when he made Henry VIII. say (Act 1, Sc. 2) : Things done without example, in their issue Are to be fear'd. Have you a precedent Of this Commission? I believe, not any. We must not rend our subjects from our laws, And stick them in our will. Where this is question'd, send our letters, with Free pardon to each man that has denied The force of this Commission. We must wait for the completion until the new Parliament, as Mr. Asquith aud Lord Randolph predict, has expunged the recent resolution from the journals of the House." Another correspondent, writing on the same subject, directs our attention to the folllowing passage irom "The Ring and the Book," x., 649: These letters, false beyond all forgery— Not just handwriting and mere authorship, But false to body and soul they figure forth.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT

TH' OWD ROCKIN' A glint at owil familiar things Brings pleasure gleoms to UV eye; For tho' Time wings, Fond memory clings To th' joys o' days gooan bye; An' cleawds o' trubble melt away Whene'er aw chance to look, An' see th' fire-leet , Reflected breet Fro' th' rockin' cheer th' nook. Its stood a lot o' wear an' tear, An' vet it's firm an' strong; Ther's nowt i bits, For o' as its Bin knocked abeawt so long. It's nod o" th' fashionable mek, Wi' fancy curve an' crook, But gradely good • Wed l polished wood,— Thad rockin' chear th' nook. Wev, fooak, id welly shines as breet As t' thowts 'at leet ml mind ; We've chears beside But that's mi pride— Another awst ne'erfind To pleos me—nowe, hod hawf as wed, For memory flings a rook • 0' thovrts o'er t' past, 'At rest at last On t' rockin' chear th' nook. Mi mother rocked me thad chear, An' on id oft aw played; An' theer hoo seet, • When aw, at net. • Knelt on her knee an' prayed. An* when ml smilin' gronny coom, Thad soot hoo allus took, Id seemed to pleos, An' aivc her eose ; Thad rockin' chear th' nook.

Hey! aw remember id wur t' throne For me—i' childish mirth; When t' mates an' me Pth' height o' glee Played babby heawse on t' hearth' An' if ml grondad camped a bit, He'd twat an' chaff an' smook, An' one day he Seed suddenly rue rockin' chear th' nook. At th' after thad—hey dear o' me I Another babby coom,' ' Aw know o'er thad, id hod a lad, For d aw d to mek room, An' mony a heawr o' t' weshin' days, Or when owt wur to cook, Aw'd child to noss— Wod cud be woss ! On t' rockin' chear th' nook. Time flew; Life's duties aw'd to face, Then t' cooartin' days begun; Th' gret word wur sed, An' we geet wed, As other fooak hey done. Eawr fooak declared they'd start me off, When th' owd hooam aw forsook, An' sed, "Heigh, Dick, Just tek thi pick ;" Aw took th' owd chear th' nook. An' theer id is—a relic owd Aw'v'e liked weel o ml life; Thad simple thing Hes t' peawr to bring Thowts keener than a knife. For them 'at's rocked in't heather names Set deawu th' sexton's book; I' th' mowd they lie, An' brass korn'd buy Th' owd rockin' chear th' nook.

div.head: FIDJIIJER JOE.
div.p: FIDJIIJER JOE.
A TOUCHING. BACKWOODS STORY.
BY CLAEiNCE EL PEARSON.

I stood by the one little square window of which good Parson Griggs' log cabin boasted, gazing dreamily out across the clearing, which seemed like a diminutive island in an ocean of pine. A heavy snow-storm had mantled every visible object with white, and the crystal flakes were still slowly sift- ing down, although the sun was driving wedges of gold through the myriad rifts that divided the sonar ber clouds overhead. ' _ _ _

" It's clarin up," remarked the parson, as he knocked the ashes out of his pipe and placed it upon the rude mantle above the fire-place. "I reckon," he continued," thet if were goin' to try an' hey' any fun with the deer to-day, we'd better turn loose the purps an' git to rackin.' " He was a curious character, was the parson, and a man of many callings. Hunter, trapper, river driver, farmer, and preacher, he was as genuine a product of Northern Michigan as the sturdy pines that hedged his forest home. True, his illiteracy may have somewhat circumscribed his usefulness as a minister of the gospel, but his hearers, for most part were not disposed to be hypercritical, and his weekly meetings at the big log school house over on section eight were well attended. He possessed a homely wit, a ready command of language, and a fund of Shrewd, practical common sense, which in a great measure atoned for deficiences in the matter of edu- cation, and he was very popular with his back- woods congregation. ' "He hadn't no college-bred pulpit-mauler," said one of his admirers to me on one occasion, "an' he dorn't use such putty language as some I've heerd, but when he gits warmed up with the spirit an' goes to showin' up the blamed dirt and meannes that most of us kerries in our hearts he made me feel meaner 'n a yaller dog—durn me if he don't."

But whatever may have been the parson's merits ordemerits as a preacher he was certainly a most excellent hunter, and every year late in the shoot- ing season I left my business and sought the pineries for a two weeks' hunt with my" eccentric friend. On the day of which 1 speak,we had been kept in the house several ,hours by the driving storm, and we hailed the prospect of pleasant weather with much 'satisfaction. "This is a mighty big fall o' snow for': November,' said the parson as he slipped a handful of cartridge into his Winchester. "an' it'll be a gret day for trackW. I

wouldn't. wonder ef--" - At this point he was interrupted by the loud baying of one of his hounds", and a moment later there came a rap at the door. The visitor without waiting for an invita- tion, strode into the cabin, and divesting himself of a big fur cap which had covered the larger share of his face, revealed the familiar features of Big John, a woodsman from one of the neighbouring camps and a well-known character in those parts. • "I've come down," said Big John, as he shook the snow from his "Mackinaw," to git vs to go up to Colburn's camp, an' I'm mighty glad I found yer to home, parson. Fiddler Joe got all smashed up this mornin' an' he wants to see yer bad." "How did it happen 2" I asked, "I vrarn't thar, said Big John," but the boys said as how two blame tools from Saginaw as was hangin' around the camp got in the way of a fallin' tree an Joe rushed in to push, them back an' got piriched him- self." _ .

"Is he bad hurt ?" asked the parson. . "He's got his sinnmons an' thar ain't no kittin round it. I'm mighty dubious that he won't hold out till we git thar," and the big fellow brushed something from his face that did not resemble snow, and turning abruptly away walked to the windoy and stood looking out in silence until we got ready to start. Fiddler Joe was a great friend of ours—indeed, he was the friend of all who knew him. Rough and uncouth in his manner, but honest, generous and true, he .was a prime favourite' with his fellow craftsmen and very popular with the settlers. He wxs an excellent per- former on the violin, and his presence was in demand at all the country dances far and wide. After a hard day's work in camp he would frequently walk several miles to gratify the wishes of some of his young friends who considered no social gathering or entertainment complete without Joe and his fiddle. His willingness to oblige, his kindness of heart and his generosity, were proverbial. If one of the boys in camp were sick, it was Fiddler Joe that nursed him back to health. If a corn-

rade was in hard luck, he was always sure of Joe's sympathy and aid. It was he who breasted the mad waters of the North Branch in the dead of winter to save a crippled chore boy from drowning. It was he too, who, when Big John came down with the smallpox in Bradford's Camp, in the spring of '79, remained with him and nursed him through his illness when every other man in the crew fled in terror at the first mention of the pestilential disease. Where he came from, or what his antecedents were, no one knew, for he never told anything of his past life, and did not like to be ques- tioned concerning it. It was believed by his friends that he had at some time occupied a much higher station in life than his present one, and there were those who said that once, when somewhat under the influence of liquor—the only time, solar as anyone knew, that he had ever yielded to any extent to the seductive influence of the flowing bowl—he had cast his rude form of speech from him as a garment, and conversed for a time in language that would have done credit to the most cultured gentleman. An hour's walk brought us to Colbuin's Camp, which was something over four miles distant. The injured man was lying on a rude couch near the doorway of the sleeping camp. It needed but a glance at his pallid , features to assure me that he was past all human aid. , The bones of his chest had been crushed and shattered ,by the terrible blow he had received, and he breathed with great difficulty. He recognised us as we entered, and feebly stretched forth his hand to welcome us. "Shall I pray with you, Joe ?" asked the parson. "Yes, parson,- answered Fiddler Joe, "but make it short, 'cause thar' ain't much time." Parson Griggs knelt beside the dying man and sent up , a petition for the soul so soon to be launched upon the boundless ocean of eternity. When he arose the men in the room and about the door were standing with un- covered heads, and the tear of sympathy gleamed on many a cheek for years unused to such a visitor. "low do you feel alocut the futur', Joe ?" asked the parson. "Is all' well with ver ?" "I guess it's all right, friend," replied doe, feebly;. "it kinder seems to me thet I've done more good than harm in the world, an' I reckon the balance 'll be on the right side. Ef I ain't squard now thar ain't no time for me to square myself." He paused fora moment to rest and then continued, " Thar's two or three things I want to talk about. As I was tellin' the boys, I don't want no tuss made, no church funeral, no grave stuns. Jest plant me out here in the woods somewhar—at the foot of some big pine. I hain't no kin as would keer for me, dead cr alive—an' I allus sleep better in the woods, any- how." He paused again, faint and weak front his effort to talk. Big John held a small flask of spirits to his lips and he revived. " I want ye to say a little suthin' at the plantin,' tar- eon," he said presently; " I don't want no sugar coatin' nor nothin' o' thet sort, but you kin jest say, an' say it truthful, too, thet I never went back on no friend —not once. Thet's why I'm here, boys—here in the pinewoods —dyin' away from my kin—jest because—l stood by—a friend—when he—" and his voice sank to an indistin- guishable whisper. " Where are your relations, Joe ?" asked the parson in husky tones, as he bent over the sufferer—" ain't thar no one ye want us to write to ?" "No," gasped Joe; "I've been—dead to them—twenty years." A spasm of pain crossed his face, his head sank back and death for ever sealed the mystery of his life.

We buried him, as he had requested, deep in the forest at the fo3t of an enormous pine. Over the open grave Parson Griggs paid a homely but touching tribute to the virtues of his dead friends, and thert knelt in prayer be- side the rude coffin. "0, Lord," hs, said, "we commend to Thy mercy the spent that went out yesterday through the gates of death into the unknown land that lays beyond.. Thou knowest that our friend was not considered as bein' a prayin' man, but we who knew him best feel sure that his heart prayed when his lips made no sound. He made no professions but we believe that Thou wilst judge him by the testimony of his acts rather than that of hi, mouth. Like hina they crucified, he died to save others. Like Him, too, he went through life doin' good. His ear was never deaf ,to the voice of trouble. He clothed the naked, fed thwhungry, an' visited the sick. No night was so dark, no storm so fierce, no road so rough, as to keep him from the side of the sufferin' an' the needy. Efe was eery man's brother. Of all who key come here to honor him that is not one whose load he has not some- time made a, littlielighter. We bury here the worthless husk that hid thet"golden grain of goodness. May we who stay4aehind larn the lessons thet his life an' death should teach. May the seeds of kindness thet lie scattered all through this forest wilderness blossom in tempted souls an' bear- fruit M for thy kingdom; an' to Thy name shall be all the glory. Amen." Three days later returning from a hunting excursion the parson ad I passed Fiddler Joe's grave. As we neared the ilia we saw Big John standing by the tall pine which was Joe's monument. He had hewn a sort of tablet on the side of the tree and stood regarding it as we came up. "He didn't want us to git him no grave stun, an' I thought thar ought to be suthin' more'n a tree to mark the grave of the whitest man that ever struck these parts," said John, as he hastily passed his sleeve across his eyes. "'Taint no very handsome job," he continued, apologetically. "but 'twas the best I knowed how to do., '

Upon the tablet rudely carved with a pocket knife was the following inscription : FIDLAR JO CURTISS, Dide Nov. 25, A.D., 1885, age 45. HE WAS A WHITE MAN FROM HIS BITTER RP. " Ov sech is the Kingdom uv Heyln." —" Detroit Free Press."

div.head: SCHOOLBOY WIT.
div.p: SCHOOLBOY WIT.

The following effort is a seleetion from a third standard lad's composition exercise upon "The Donkey," Only the first two paragraphs of the essay are omitted: "The Donkey is one of that tribe of beasts on which the cane has no effekt, for the harder you hit it the slower it goes. Your fathers never use a whip for there donkeys, becase they no it would not hurt them. For the Donkey rather likes to feel a whip, as it only tikles him and makes him feel joyfull and hungry. The best _thing to punish a Donkey with is firstly a short thick cane for ear d and holly; and secundly, a broomstick cut in two for backbone and back legs. He will then I go betwixt four and five miles an hour. The donkeys ' which you see painted yellow and blue on the school pictures are what are called jew's asses. These tribes of donkeys go many miles an hour, and will follow there masters like dogs and lambs becose of kindness. The young ones are sometimes called kolts and foals of asses. Therefore, if you have aniced young donkey show mercy unto it, and it might grow into a kelt or the foal of an ass. There is also the tribe of wild asses which prowl upon the top of rocks, and never slip over, even in winter. Tney are larger than our moddern donkeys, and surer footed. In the night time they climb down, and feed like rab- bits upon the poor farmer's hard earned vegitebles," The branch of secular work which children abhor more than any other is beyond a doubt " grammar and analysis." I have frequently noticed that dur- ing this lesson the lads grow restless and even irrit- able, and the discipline becomes, in consequence, more difficult to maintain. Hence, I can very well understand that irritableness, quite as much as ignorance, was the cause of the startling answer given by a north-country lad to his inspector din-- ing an examination in grammar. The inspector was dealing with the genders of nouns and pronouns, and amongst other questions, he asked : " What is the gender of the noun egg ?" " Sir," answered a tall, shrewd lad behind, who probably surmised that it was a kind of" catch " question, and was deter- mined to prove himself equal to the occasion, "you canna tell till it's hatched !" The next selection is taken from the essay of a lad in the third standard of the school, the subject for a composition being "Coals." Here ia the third paragraph of the lad's exercise :" Be sure also at all times not to waste those coals which your Mother have to work so hard for in washing. For your Mother cant spare more than 3 pence a day out of 2 and 9 pence, with cloths and boots to. buy, and the rent, and all " that bread-and all the herrins which you eat. Be sure and not light the fire till she comes home at night, but keep yourselves warm by playing in the street, or when its wet, running up and down the stares quick. Also blowing hands and jumping." Some years ago I had occasion to pay a visit to St. Mary's College, Hammersmith, a most excellent institution for the training of Roman Catholic students for the office of schoolmaster. Whilst there the following anecdote was related to me by a student. The worthy master of a poor Catholic school situated in one of the lowest parts of the metropolis, took " The Sea" as the subject of a "Friday afternoon," lesson. In the course of the lesson he asked, "What should you think it is, my lads, which makes the sea so salt ?" Presently, a little collarless and shoeless' urchin raised his hand and answered, "Soldiers and bloaters, sir ? " "Soldiers," it appears, is the popu- lar name for red herrings.—Henry .T. Barker, in Longman's Magazine.

div.head: CHAPTER VI.
div.p: CHAPTER VI.

DURK BEES HIS WAY MIA% "rfaavousms from want of tone" was the dodoes verdict upon Ruth Lister's ailment, and the remedies prescribed had for principal absolute mental repose. This and a young healthy constitution soon restored her; so that in less than a month after poor Mrs. Woolford's funeral she was downstairs, looking so sweet and pure in her simple mourning that Mark Woolford's heart used to neat heavily in her presence, and many a passionate and loving thought was hidden , beneath themask of coldness which he wore. I All in due course Miss Klopstock had arrived in a , slab "red hot," Martin said, about the sundry belong- ings that she intended to bring. I "I engaged the man only after inquiring a great ' deal about his character," said Miss Klopstock, seating herself in the first chair she came to, just as Mark and , his brother were sitting down to dinner one evening. " Is anything wrong?" exclaimed Mark, eagerly. " Wrong ? Yes, everything's wrong," exclaimed Miss Klopstock, excitedly. ' Where are my things?" "I thought they were coming in a van," said Mark, " So's Christmas coming," cried the lady, tartly.

"In a van ?" said Mar'iin. "I was not speaking to you, young man," said Miss lalopstock, sharply. "I suppose you think that's very clever, sir? but I don't." "Are they on the way?" asked Mark. "1 don't know," cried the lady. I engaged the rascal to fetch them in a lock-up van, and when it came it was all open, and the impudent fellow declared that I never said a word stout a lock-up van, but, if I liked, he'd lock one of the wheels. / don't know what he meant." "And did he take the boxes and things?" "Yes, and where's he taken thsati to? That's what I want to know," cried the poor woman, wiping her face. "Oh, I should think he'll be hero soon," said Mark. "Ann, will you take Miss Klopstock's bonnet?" "No, no; not yet, my dear. I couldn't take off a thing till I know that my boxes are here safely. I arranged it all so perfectly that he should get here when you were at home, so that there might be no trouble and abuse over the paying, and now I want to know where the things have gone. I wouldn't lose those boxes for the world." "Sit down and have some dinner, and they'll be here by that time." "Oh, dear no," cried Miss Klopstock, shaking her head violently; "and Ws my belief that they never will come. No; I shall never set eyes upon those

boxes again—never." _ "Here they are," said Martin, with a sneer. "No ; I don't believe it. They're gone. I'm sure they are gone," cried the lady, piteously. "The rascal of a man knew that they were valuable. All my jewellery and both my go)cl watcheB are in the black leather case; and I've got some money there, too, for there isn't a bank you can trust nowadays." Martin glanced at her sidewise eiR she said tivese last words, and then seemed to be listening to thi, noise outside. For a van had stopped at the door, and the maid mine back after a few minutes' absence to say that Miss Klopstock's things had arrived. "Then I don't believe they'll be half of them th,re,- cried the lady, and it was not until every box and case bad been examined and checked twice over that she would consent to sit down to dinner. "I don't like these strange men," she said, as she grew a little cooler. "I think that— Oh, gracious! It never occurred to me before," she cried, srarting uj from the table; "I'll be bound to say every box ha. been wrenched open." "Well, let's go and see," said Mark, smiling as Is rose, and took Mies Klopstock into the hall. "Old cat!" muttered Martin, impatiently, as he rose, went to the other end of the table, and helpei himself to all the gravy. • " Thank you, Mark. It's very, very good of you,' said Miss Kliipstock, returning to the dining.room. "Moving does upset me so, and one is surrounded by such..a pack of wicked wretches that one never feels

safe." After this Miss Klopstock settled down, and after a consul'ation between her bro'ber and Mark respecting a rather implement little ezpose that had coin° to the manager's ears just about the time of Mrs. Woolford's death, Martin, who knew of the com,ultation, and that a sum of money must hare been paid, because be was not asked for it any mere, seemed to have settled down as well, and there was comparative peace in Bruns- wick-square. It took Miss Klopstcck quite a fortnight to get regularly settled, but after that period she seemed regularly at home, much to the disgust of Martin, who lost no opportunity of trying to annoy her. He made such remarks as would have driven mast women from the house, but Miss Klopstock 0013 tightened her lips and remained silent. Upon several occasions Mark had hard work to restrain himself, for he could so that his brother was growing more offensive from the impunity be enjoyed itt, home, while a pang went to the sleler's heart as he saw how thoroughly Ruth sided with the offender. " I am very sorry, Miss Kopstock," said Mark one evening after a rather unp7t.asent scene, "and I feel as if I ought to do someth;ng to check ell this, but Z. want to _win Martin. and kindii.ss if lean"

. ..... _ _ _ "Humph! yes," said Miss Klopstoek. "1 salvors you are right, and if you gave him whip or spur he would gallop off to destruction." "I hope not," said Mark, with a sigh; "but I feat coercion would do no-good. Kindness must win him in the end."

"Never." said Miss Morita, firmly. "Look here, Mart, I speak out my mind because I like you, and and I'm not afraid of your being offended. it will take something stronger than you can give to cure him."
"Oh, no; theses taking a very hard view of the ease," said Mark; "but I'm very vary sorry that matters are made so unpleasant for you, who have so

. - kindly eome to our help. 71 "Unpleasant! For me r echoed Mies Klopstock, looking excessively acid as she spoke. "Why. my dear Mark, I like it.. I haven't been so happy for years." "Happy r exclaimed Mark. "To be sure. Happy. Why, my dear boy, there's nothing I enjoy better than a little tiff. It was terribly dull before I came here." Ohe tried to smile, but it was not a satisfactory effort, and it would not have been taken for a pleasant look by any one who did not know the lady. Then she stood by the mantelpiece smoothing down her black silk apron and went on— " The fact is, Mark, that boy don't like my being here, and be has made up his mind to worry me into going away, and Fm not going to let him do it." "Let's try and be as charitable to him as we can, Miss Klopstock." "Oh, yes, well be charitable, Mark; but there are bounds to everything. You fee he finds me an obstacle in the way of his making love to little Ruth, and Bless and save the man, what is the matter?" Mark had started violently at her words; but ha now smiled and tried to shake it off. "Nothing!" he said; "a sort of spasm, that's all. I'm better now." " Ah, I know the. sensation exactly," said Miss Klopstock, nodding her head. "If you feel it again six drops of camphorated spirit on a lump of sugar will do you no end of good." "Do you—do you think that Ruth eaves for him?" said Mark, speaking huskily, and trying hard to look oomposed. " A silly girl: yes," exclaimed Miss Klopstock. "It's always the way and always was. So sure as there's a black lamb in a family the mother worships it. If a man is decidedly vicious—" She pointed all this out, forefinger upon her left hand, as if checking the matter off. "I say if there's a man decidedly vicious, the sweetest and truest and best girl in the neighbourhood is sure to take a fancy to him. I thank my stars I never thought about such stuff." "Does—does Martin pay her much attention ?" faltered Mark. "Yes, when I'm there." said Miss Klopstock, with an angry snap. "He seed I don't like it,and so he goes on the more. Tchah: I haven't pat,ence with such rubbish." "But does he pay her this attention when Miss Klopstock is not there?" Mark Woolford asked him- self, as be sat there very moody and thoughtful. "I can't think how Ruth caa like him,' kdded the lady. "If he does really love her," thought Mark, after as interval of silence, full of intense pain," it will be his salvation:" and though the feeling of utter despair and blankness which 'Famed to come upon him threatened his future like a storm-cloud, he recalled the deathbed of his mother, and his promise, telling himself tint his life must be one of self- sacrifice, and that he must make a strong effort to meet in h manly spirit what evidently was to be his fate. For he argued if Martin really loved Ruth, she, in her sweet purity of heart,would win him ton better life, for, in spite of past known enls to themselves

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE 'OF LORDS.—DIONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. TRUST COMPANIES BILL.The Trust Companies Bill passed through committee after the insertion of 'a clause, on the motion of the Lord Chancellor, limiting trust companies from engaging in business outside of their trusts. FAMINE AT SUAKIM.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, reply- ing to the Earl of Dundonald, stated that no doubt the famine was very severe in the neighbourhood of Suakim, but there was no precedent for the purpose of feeding a foreign population. OVERWORK IN COLLIERIES.—The Earl CPI DUNRAVEN called attention to the conviction at Pontypridd of a man named Rowlands for a breach of the special rules of the National Colliery. Rowlands, who was in charge of a ventilating fan, had been overworked, having been en- gaged fourteen and a half hours on the day the offence was committed, and being exhausted he had fallen asleep. Lord DE RAMSEY' replying on behalf of the Home Office, said that neither the general rules laid down in the Coal Mines Regulation Act of 1887, nor the special rules established in the South Wales district, had attempted to regulate the number of hours to be worked by men in charge of steam machinery. The House adjourned at 25 minutei to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAT.

The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. AFRICAN LIQUOR TRAFFIC.—Sir JAMES FERGUSSON, answering Mr. Howorth, said the policy of the Niger Company had been to limit the spirit trade in the Ldwer Niger, and as far as possible to check altogether the importation of spirits into the Mussulman territories on the Central Niger and Benire. THE ABSENT MEMBER.—Mr. W. H. SMITH having had 'his attention called by Mr. Cobb to the prolonged absence from the House of Mr. Kynoch, the member for the Aston Division, said he regretted the prolonged absence of any supporter of the Government. No doubt other members were also absent. He understood Mr. Kynoch would return shortly, and did not see that he was ct Red upon to interfere between members and their consti- tuents. THE WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING COMMISSION.—MT. 0. BIORGAN : I beg to ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he can now state when the report of the Royal Commission on the operations of the Sunday Closing (Wales) Act, IsBl, will be issued. Mr. MATTHEWS : The report has been signed by the Chair- man, and is now being signed by the other commis- sioners, some of whom were in the country. It will be in the printers hands in about a week, and its issue may be expected shortly after. Tan Never, ESTIMATES.—A discussion having taken place on a proposal of Mr. Gourley to appoint a select copmittee to inquire into the designs under which vetsele of war are being built and equipped for the navy, the House went into committee on the naval estimates, the remainder of the evening being occupied in the con- sideration of the naval votes. Inuit BOARDS OF CrUIRDIANS.—MT. HOWARTH asked the Attorney-General for Ireland if he would give the names of the Board of Guardians in Irelapd which had been dissolved during the last 10 years, with the locali- ties in which they were situated ?—The ATTORNEY- GENERAL for IRELAND: The fallowing are the names of the Boards of Guardians which have been dissolved dur- ing the past ten years, and the counties in which they are situated—Bellmullett, county Mayo, dissolved twice; Swineford, Mayo, twice; Newport, Mayo, once ; Car- rick-on-Suir, Tipperary, Once; New Ross, Wexford, once ; Ballinasloe, Galway, once; Athy, Kildare, once; Dungarvan Waterford, once ; Ballyvagham, Clare, once: Portuma, Galway, once : Cork, once. INFANT LIFE PROTECTION BILL.—MT. W. H. SMITH moved the second reading of the Infant Life Protection J. BELLY condemned the Bill as one which made it impossible for friendly neighbours to take care of children for a few hours without being registered as baby-farmers. It was a Bill for the persecution of honest poor children. He appealed to the House to post- pone the second reading in consideration of what its effect would be. He moved the adjournment of the debate. The motion was negatived without a division. The Bill was ultimately read a second time, and referred to a Select Committee. Miscettsireous.—The Crown Office Bill was read a second time. The Hares Preservation Bill was read a second time. • The House adjourned at five minutes to one o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the wool sack at half-past five o'clock. COLONIAL COURTS ADMIRALTY BILL.—The Colonial Courts ot Admiralty Bill passed through the Committee stage, and the Indian Councils Bill was read a third time aid passed. The sitting only lasted ten minutes. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEsnas.

_ The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. NEW WRIT.—On the motion of Mr. AKERS DOUGLAS, a new writ was ordered to be made out for East Down, Ireland, for the election of a member in the place of Mr. Richard Ker, resigned. PRIVATE BUSINESS.—Private businessoccupied upwards of two hours, the Landon County Council Bill and the London Street Improvement Bill giving rise to consider- able discussion. ENGLAND AND SWAZILAND.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, reply- ing to a question, said it would be a breach of the con- vention of 1884 to establish the British protectorate over Swaziland without the consent ot the South African Republic. MINING DISASTERS AND COMPENSATION.—Mr. SAMUEL EVANS asked whether, in view of the great distress caused by disasters in mines, the Government would give facili- ties for the passing of a short measure to provide for the ' payment by royalty owners of 2 per cent, to a national fund to relieve such distress.—Mr. W. H. SMITH said he could give no pledge in regard to a Bill which might seriously affect the relations between employers and em- ployed, and tend to diminish the spontaneous generosity of the public. TER BERLIN :LABOUR:CONFERENCE.—The First Lord of the Treasury, replying to Mr. Atherley-Jones, denied that any distinction had been made between the classes of persons who represented this codntry at the Berlin Labour Conference. The plenipotentiaries had been appointed because of their general knowledge of the question to be dealt with, and the experts had been chosen because of their special acquaintance with particular trades and industries. FORTHCOMING BlL\9.—The Scotch and English Bills respecting the education of the blind and deaf, it was elicited would shortly be introduced in the House of Lords, but Mr. W. H. Smith could hold out no hopes that the Employers' Liability Bill would be taken before Easter. PUBLIC RIGHTS IN SCOTLAND.—DEFEAT OF THE GOVERN- NENT.—Mr. Bucneweis called attention to the constant enroachment on, and loss of, public rights of way in Scotland, and moved that the duty of maintaining them be entrusted to the County Councils —Mr. Mixes seconded.—The LORD-ADVOCATE, in the course Of the debate, said the Government were willing to take into consideration representations that public rights of way were being lost with a view to seeing whether means for their protection could not be devised, but beyond I that he was not prepared to go .—On a division the Government sustained their second defeat this session, the voting being—for the motion 110, against 97. A COUNT OCT.—During the consideration of the Direc- tors' Liability Bill the House was counted out at ten minutes to eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. Prayers were said soon after twelve o'clock in the presence of the Speaker and four members. BANKRUPTCY LAW.—Sir ALBERT ROLLIT moved the second reading of the Bankruptcy Bill, and in the course of his remarks said the Bill was based essentially on . the principles of the Act a 1883, and with one or two excep- tions would be found not to contain any departure from then prNciples. One of the clauses sought to render a bankrupt in future punishable for misdemeanour under the Debtors Act of 1869—that was to say, for Wale ing goods on credit by fraudulent misrepresentation or false pretences, or for pawning or pledging goods obtained on credit and not paid for. Mr. KELLY moved, and Sir J. M'KEENA seconded, that the bill be read a second time that day six months, but the amendment was negatived without a division, and the bill was ordered to be re- ferred to the Standing Comtnittee on Trade. LEASEHOLDERS (IRELAND) BILL.—Mr. T. P. O'CozomE, in moving the second reading of the Leaseholders' , (Ireland) Bill, explained that its object was to extend to all leaseholders in Ireland the right of going before the Lan Court to have a fair rent fixed. Mr. T. W. Russell was in favour of the principle of the bill, and Mr. Balfour said he could not acquit perpetuity leaseholders of culpable negligence when they for ever .bound them- selves to pay a full rent for agricaltural land. The de- bate on the bill stood adjourned at half-past five, and the report of supply was brought up and agreed to, , with the exception of one Navy vote. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TwonsnAv.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. 'Lord Stratheden reintroduced his Bill for the preven- tionof smoke in the metropolis. Lord KNUMFORD, in reply to the Earl of Meath, assented to a return being made regarding the means adopted in the colonies for the transport of civilian sick and injured, the object being to direct attention to the absence in this country of any organised system. Lord Cranbrook assented to a suggestion by Lord Sandhurst, that a Select Corn. mittee should be app•Dinted with regard to all hospitals, dispensaries, and charitable institutions within the metropolitan_ area. Their lordships rose at ten minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THITESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Mr. COURTNEY moved the appoint- ment of a Select Cornrnitttee to consider various bills dealing with the conversion of railway stock. There were many questions asked, and these included inquiries as to the tests for colour blindness in the mercantile marine, the establishment of lobster factories on the Newfoundland shore, sentences at quarter sessions, and also as to affairs in Swaziland and in Crete. Mr. SMITH could not say anything definite about the Easter recess, except that the Irish Land Bill would have to be intro- duced and the Tithes Bill read a second time before there
LORD SALISBURY'S 'VISIT TO THE QUEEN.

Lord Salisbury wont to Windsor on Wednesday after- noon for the purpose of having an audience of her Majesty in connection with State affairs previous to her departure for the Continent. The fact of his lordship visiting the Queen at this juncture, it is stated, has no political significance, but is in the ordinary course of business. According to the latest arrangements, Lord Salisbury will leave London for the Continent before Saturday week, the 29th inst.

div.head: DUKE OF EDINBURGH IN A FIT.
div.p: THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH IN A FIT.

When the Duke of Edinburgh was absent from the late King of Portugal's funeral, some surprise was expressed, but no reason was given. The following remarkable ' story is now told of the matter. The Duke had prepared to go to the funeral. He had just taken his leave of the King and was crossing the grand vestibule Of the palace to his carriage, when he fell to the ground in a fit of epilepsy, and began to dash his head against the marble floor. So startled and terrified were the Portuguese chamberlains and dignitaries in attendance by the con- tortions of his features and limbs that it was not until sharply rebuked by the Duke's equerry that they recovered their presence of mind sufficiently to lend a helping hand. In the meantime, however, the prostrate man had been permitted to bruise his face in such a manner as to render any appearance in public for several days absolutely out of the question. As soon as the fit had passed off, he returned to the Palace of Necessidades, and on the following morning, while the entire popula- tion was gazing at the funeral prccession, and wonder- ing at his absence, he drove down to the arsenal, and quietly wont on board the Active, where he spent the remainder of the day in the congenial society of his old messmates. To such an extent were his features dis- figured and discolored from the effects of his fall, that he was forced to remain a full week at Lisbon before being able to start on his return journey.—The Star. .

div.head: LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL DEFENDS
div.p: LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL DEFENDS
HIMSELF.

------- Writing to the " Morning Post" on Monday, Lord R. Churchill says : Having received several communications requesting me to publish the memorandum on the Special Commis- sion which I wrote and submitted to Mr. Smith on the 17th July, 1888, I shall be much obliged to you if you can find space for it in your columns. On the day above-mentioned I was informed on good authority that there was a prospect of the Government reconsidering their policy with respect to the Commis- sion, for the constitution of which a Bill had been intro- duced on the 16th of July. The Bill had not been printed and circulated, and no appreciable discussion had taken place. It must be remembered that at that time the Special Commission was offered as a free gift to the Irish party, to be taken er rejected, and on one—not even the Ministers themselves—dreamed that the closure would be resorted to for the purpose of forcing the pro- posed tribunal upon the accused parties. Indeed the Government had intimated that in the event of the Bill leading to protracted debate it would not be persevered with. Under these circumstances the memorandum in question was hastily written, and was intended to be a strong but friendly protest against the measure. The speech which I delivered in the House of Commons on Tuesday last was intended to be the strongest possible protest which it was in my power to make against any such measure being ever proposed by a Government to Parliament again. I observe that by certain organs of opinions I am accused on account of that speech of disloyalty to the Unionist party. I wholly fail to perceive in what manner the two protests for which I am responsible, and which must be taken together, form any foundation for such a charge. Indeed, my want of perception in this matter is so remarkable that it even occurs to me that the charge of disloyalty to the Unionist party might be more forcibily urged against those who, in spite of every warn- ing, persisted in proposing to and forcing upon Parlia- ment the unfortunate measure in question, which by its history and its results has most obviously dealt a heavy blow at the cause and party of the Union. The memorandum mentioned is alengthy one, and sets forth the righthon. gentleman's objections tothe Govern- ment policy.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 22, 18
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 22, 18

TiiE RESIGNATION OF PRINCE BISMARK. ) COLOGNE, WEDNESDAY.—The Kolische Zeitung" of this evening published the following telegram from Ber- lin :—The Emperor this afternoon accepted the resigna- tion of Prince Bismark, whith was tendered to his Majesty in a document of 20 pages setting forth his reasons for the step. The Imperial decree formally noti- fying the Emperor's acceptance of the Chancellor's re- signation will probably be drawn up even before the end of the day. It is declared on. trustworthy authority, that General Von Caprivi has signified his acceptance of the Imperial request that he should sueceed Prince Bis- mark. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY..— The Emperor William this morning gave audience to the ,Minister Herr von Boet- ticher, and later on he conferrld with General Caprivi, the former chief of the Imperial Admiralty. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY, 5 e.g.—Since a quarter-past three o'clock this afternoon a council of Ministers, over which Herr Von Boetticher is presiding, has been sitting in one of the committee rooms of the Prussian Lower House. BERLIN,WEDNRSDAY, 5-30 P. m.--,-This evening's National Zeitung states that it learns from a trustworthy source that General Von Caprivi is designated as Prince Bis- mark's successor in the Imperial Chancellorship, and apparently also in the post of President of the Imperial Ministry. Count Herbert Bismark, adds the paper, is determined to go out of officewith his father, and he will probably be replaced in the post of Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs by Herr Von Radowitz, the German Ambassador at Constantinople, or Count Hatzfeldt, the Ambassador in London. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY tVENING.—The announcement of the appointment of General Von Caprivi to succeed Prince Bismark as Imperial Chancellor now only awaits official confirmation. It may also be regarded as certain that Count Herbert Bismark has resigned, and it is stated that he will receive an ambassadorial appointment. The choice of his successor at the Foreign Office is thought to lie between Count Munster, German Ambas- sador in Paris, and Herr Von Radowitz and Count Hatzfeldt. Herr Von Boetticher, the present Vice-Presi- dentef the Prussian Ministry and Secretary of State for the Interior, is designated for the post of Prbsitlent in succession to Prince Bismark. He will be replaced in the secretaryship of the Interior by Count Enlenberg, Governor of Hesse-Nassau. The resignation is also reported of Herr Herrfurth, Minister of the Interior, and of Herr Von Maybach, Minister of Public Works, who, owing to the retirement of Prince Bismark, has, it is alleged, lost his support against the demands for increased means of communication for strategic pur- poses.

div.head: MORFA COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: THE MORFA COLLIERY DISASTER.

The Morfa pit is again on fire, and the work of recover- ing the bodiesis suspended. The bodies recovered now number 42. The manager of the pit has made a state- ment as to the alleged use of dynamite, contradicting in a large measure the allegations which have obtained currency. Owing to the fire, all hope of recovering any additional bodies has been abandoned. A consultation between Mr. Gray, themanager, and three other mining engineers has been held, and it was decided as a last resort to flood the mine. Preparations for this work have been begun, and it may be assumed that this deter- mination means the closing of the pit. Sixteen funerals took place on Saturday, and ten or twelve on Sunday. The scenes witnessed were of a sad and mournful description. Miss Talbot, of Margam Castle, has contri- buted £2,500, Miss Olive Talbot £5OO, and Mrs. Fletcher £5O to the Morfa Colliery Relief Fund.

div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

TWO SOLDIERS DROWNED. Sergeant Lunin and Corporal Considine, on the Man- chester Regiment, stationed at Rocky Island, Queens- town, were drowned on Sunday evening by the capsiz- ing of a pleasure boat. THE TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT.

Archbishop Croke has issued an address to the mem- bers of the Gaelic Athletic Association, exhorting them to join the Father Mathew Temperance Association next Sunday in their respective parishes. THREE BOYS DROWNED. Two youths named Henry and George Harris, aged seven and nine, sons of a labourer, were drowned in the Dodder, at Ballsbridge, near DiAblin, on Sunday, and also a third bey whose body has not been recovered. They were playing football in a field, when they were chased by a constable, and in attempting to cross the river on the stepping-stones were washed away. A GHASTLY HOAX. ..

--- The people are laughing over a ghastly discovery made by Head Constable Walsh. Whilst walking over the bridge at Kilkenny he observed floating down the river a parcel exactly resembling a human body, mutilated after the fashion of " Jack the Ripper," and clothed in a green and yellow jersey. The Head Constable procured a boat and secured the supposed corps. On the bindings being unloosed, a number of dead pups were dis- closed. THE CHARGE OF PARRICIDE IN TIPPERARY. At the County Tipperary Assizes on Saturday, before i Chief Baron Palles, the hearing of the case n which young Dillon was charged with the murder of his father two years ego was resumed. The Judge referred to the evidence in, detail, and without calling on counsel for the prisoner to conclude the defence, directed the jury to return a verdict of acquittal. The prisoner was discharged, • and left the court accompanied by his relative. ALLEGED THREAT TO MURDER A DAUGHTER.

-- At Dublin, on Wednesday, Simon Ledwidge was charged with threatening to murder his daughter, Chris- tina Ledwidge, aged nineteen, at their residence in Newmarket, on Tuesday ; and prisoner's son was charged with brutally assaulting the girl. Evidence was given that the elder prisoner entered the room where the girl had taken refuge with her child, and threatened to take her life. The girl, to escape him, jumped from the win- dow, sustaining severe injuries. The son is alleged to have kicked her.—The accused were remanded.

FUNERAL 'OF THE LATE CANON HOPWOOD.

- - The remains of the late Canon Hopwood, M.A., were interred in Winwick churchyard, on Saturday afternoon. The ceremony was witnessed by a large gathering of people. The funeral cortege left Win- wick Hall, the late residence of the deceased, at twelve o'clock, and although there were several car- riages in the procession, only the lady mourners rode to the church. The mourners were the Rev. F. E. and Mrs. Hopwood (son and daughter-in-law of the deceased) ; Major Hopwood (son); Mr. C. A. Hop- wood (son) ; the Dean of Chester (the Van. John Lionel Darby, M.A.) ; Mrs. Darbv ; the Archdeacon of Lancas- ter (the Yen. W. Hornby) ; the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Vicar of Fluyton (a nephew of the deceased, and a for- mer curate of Winwick) ; the Rev. Canon Hornby, the Rev. John Cross: the Rev. Canon Heron (Daresbury), the Rev. Edmund Phipps Stanley, M.A. (Rector of Woot- ton, Courtney, Dunster) ; Viscount Downe, Viscount Molyneux, Admiral G. Elornby, Mr. E. Lester Pearhyn, Mr. C. A. Bagott, Mr. E. Hornby (Dalton Hall), and Captain Stanley. Lord Derby and Lord Sefton were unable to be present, the former owing to duties con- nected with the House of Lords, and the latter owing to indisposition. The funeral procession was met in the road near the north side of the church by Mr. Joseph Swinton (the late Rector's warden), Mr. J. E. Worsley (parishioners' warden), and others, as well as by the fol- lowing local tenant farmers—Messrs. James Kerfoot, James Warburton (Dallam), E. C. Cooper, Thomas War- burton, R. Pollitt, N. Byrom, P. Longton, H. Penning- ton, J. Blackledge, J. Brock, T. Mather, George Pow!. son, A. Alker, J. Dumbell, J. Unsworth, T. Ker- foot, and S. Jepson. Amongst those who also witnessed the funeral ceremony either in the church or at the grave side, were the Rev. Dr. Black, the Rev. R. Smith (Rector of St. Luke's, Lowton), the Rev. H. Monk (Newton- le-Willows), the Rev. G. Feather (vicar of Glaze- bury), the Rev. T. P. Kirkman (Croft), the Rev. W. R. H. Pughe (Newton-in-Makerfield), Rev. E. J. Hack (Wargrave), the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis), the Rev. G. F. Roberts (Hollinfare), the Rev. Morley Stevenson (Training College, Warrington), the Rev. J. J. Langham (Padgate), Rev. S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's, Warrington), the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (Holy Trinity, Warrington), the Rev. J. G. Richards (St. Anne's, Warrington), the Rev. T. Emmott (curate St. Paul's, Warrington) ; the Rev. Isaac Phillips (Orford) ; ILady Greenall, Dr. White (Warrington), Dr. Watkins (Newton-le-Willews), Captain Withington, Mr. T. Corn- -1 her, Mr. W. F. Gooch, Mr. T. H. Lyon (Appleton Hall), Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. 3. R. Buckton, Mr. R. Hood Wright ; Mr. Williams (clerk to the Leigh Local Board), Mr. H. J. Longton, Mr. Lawton, (Golborne), Messrs. C. Twiss, B. Hodgins, and G. Riley (Warrington). At the church door the procession was met by the Rev. Canon Penrhynand the Rev. J. Carson, M.A., curate of Win- wick, and the last-named gentleman commenced to read the first part of the burial service,the organist (Mr. John Kerfoot) as the mourners and others took their seats playing the Dead March in "Saul." The Rev. Canon Peurhyn coaducted the service inside the church, which was filled, a large number of the parishioners being pre- sent. The body was laid in a plain earth grave- on the south side of the church, next to the grave in which the remains of the late Lady Ellinor Hopwood wereinterred, in September, 1887. The coffin was supplied by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnstone,lcabinet makers, &c. of Bridge. St. and Rylands-st., Warrington, to whom tile whole of the funeral arrangements had also been entrusted. It was of brown oak with plain brass mountings, and on a brass plate was the inscription—" Frank George Hop- wood, born 2nd August, 1810, died March 11th, 1890, aged 80 years." The following is a list of the ladies and gentlemen who had forwarded floral wreaths: Miss Hopwood, Mrs. Darby, Mrs. C. A. Hopwood, Mrs. Henry Fielden, Miss Darby, Mr. W. Lowe, Miss Cooper (of the Seaman's Orphanage, Liverpool), the tenant farmers of the Win- wick estate, the parishioaers of St. Oswald's, and the authorities of the Warrington Training College and the Clergy Daughters' School. PULPIT REFERENCE.

On Sunday morning a large congregation assembled in St. Oswald's Church, Winwick, when reference was made from the pulpit to the death of the Rev. Canon Hopwood. Mourning was generally worn by those present. The service was conducted by the Rev. James Carson' curate of the parish, in accordance with the ancient customs of this church. The hymns sung were—" Let saints on earth in concert sing," and "Through all the changing scenes of life." The sermon was also preached by Mr. Carson, from the text "Remember them that have the rule over you," or "your guides which spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life imitate their faith." The service in the afternoon was also conducted by the Rev. J. Carson, but only a slight reference was made to the death of Canon Hopwcod. SALE OF THE HALL AND ESTATES. . .

The Bishop of Liverpool proposes to hold a confirma- tion in the church early in April, for which nearly 60 candidates are under instruction. The churchwardens, Messrs. Joseph Swinton and James E. Worsley. have been appointed sequestrators during the vacancy, the present curate continuing in charge. The population of the parish itself is about 700, but counting all who look to this as their place of worship, and are pastorally visited, there are 900 practically within the cure. The new Rectory, built by the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, will be ready for occupation, after papering and paint- ing has been completed. The hall and estate, purchased by Sir John Stanley from the monks of Nostell, in York- shire, in 1433, and since enjoyed by the rectors, will be for sale by the Commissioners. Thus will be terminated that which has been a unique parochial arrangement in the Church of England for over four centuries and a half—the late Rector having been the last of about 20 clergytnen of high position who were also lords of the manor. Whilst many deprecated the removal of such an ancient landmark, there can be no doubt that the exi- gencies of modern times, and the increased populations of the daughter parishes of Winwick, have rendered this redistribut on of its revenues necessary. Many will, however, be glad to know that some provision has been made, from these, for maintaining the fabric of the ancient church, endeared to so many, as well by: other associations because of the burial ground containing the mortal part of some of their kindred. We understand that applications for certificates from the registers,which date from 1583, are frequently made from most distant places, sometimes from America—and visitors from that country and from Australia sometimes visit the church during the summer.

WARRINGTON BEATS SEFTON HALL.

The Sankey-st., circus NVO3 again crowded on 'Saturday evening, when the Warrington eight, after defeating Exeter Hall and Bournemouth, met Sefton riall in the semi-final round in the gymnastic com- petition for the National Physical Recreation Society's 200 guineas challenge shield. The result was that the Warrington men were again victorious. Amongst those present were the Rev. C. E. Jackson, Mr. Thomas Morris, Alderman Sutton, Alderman Wright, Councillors W. Pierpoint, R. T. Fairclough, Fleming, Hutchinson, Heaton, and Hepherd; Messrs. Daniel Jones, H. Ferguson, T. B. Kiernan, J. Lyon Whittle, J. Evans, W. H. Robinson and H. Evans (lion. secretary.) With one exception—James Holmes in place of Locker, who had been injured— the Warrington team was the same as that which beat Bournemouth a fortnight ago. Before the contest began pianoforte selections were played by Mr. George Riley. The accompaniments to the subsequent bar-bell exercises were played by Mr. C. H. Singleton (Sefton Hall), and Mr. B. Wright (War- rington.) Mr. C. M. Roberts (Ancoats Gymnasium) officiated as judge. Mr. E. Alexander was director of the Warrington team, and Mr. E. A. Jones of the Sefton team.

div.head: COMPETITIONS.
div.p: THE COMPETITIONS.

The competitions were similar to those witnessed when Warrington met Bournemouth. In the bar-bell exercise Warrington were awarded 92 out of a possible 96 marks, against 88 scored by their opponents. The visitors com- piled a total of 571 on the parallel bars, but the War- rington team again showed superiority, making 61 marks. The ultimate result of the contest was made apparent when the two teams tackled the high jump. The Warrington men are very strong in this respect, and a glance at the individual scores given below will show that they had by far the best of it all through. Mason was the only Sefton Hall man who made any- thingof a show, and he stayed in the competition near- ly to the end, gaining 11 out of a possible 12 marks. For Warrington, however, J. Podmore made the full number, and received quite an ovation, whilst James Holmes had 10 marks. The Sefton Hall team had slightly the best of it in the rope-climbing contest. In the end War- rington were victorious by a substantial majority, the totals being—Warri.,gton 2661 marks ; Sefton Hall, 231 i marks. The following were the individual scores :

The final will probably be played on the 3rd Saturday in April, either at Liverpool or London.
ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE,

On Tuesday a Nottingham miner named Thomas Pearson, after retiring to rest, suddenly jumped up and with a fender murderously assaulted ha wife, to whom he was only recently married. He then attempted suicide, but was secured. The woman will recover.

div.head: MURDERER LYSCHED.
div.p: A MURDERER LYSCHED.

On Sunday a man who had committed a murder was being taken to gaol at Bloomfield, Nebraska, when he was set upon by an infuriated crowd, who overpowered the officers of the law escorting him and hanged the man within thirty minutes of the commission of the crime.

THE EXAMINER, _. BATURDAY. MARCH 22, 1890.

The History THE present is so much with usi of and it presents itself, especiallY 00 Lancashire. the political side, with so much. sound and stir, that it is pleasant nbd, and age.F.l to look upon the past through the pages of histOrfr Lancashire has for many centuries occupied a minent position in historical records, and it is stli; noted as a county which is full to over-flowing cu vital energy. This fact is strikingly apparent, those who are perusing, as it is issued from le', press, the new edition of Bairies's "History of the" County. Palatine and Duchy of Lancaster." We, have recently received from the printer and hsher (Mr. JOHN HEYWOOD, Manchester), thi! third volume of this monumental work. Theret every evidence in the latest issue that the cultureu editor, Mr. JAMES CROSTON, F.S.A., is continUi* that needful process of careful revision and exter, sive enlargement which marked the eartr volumes. A county history to be ,of highest value as a work of reference 027, " be brought, as this is, down to date. This thuu. volume continues the history of the Hundred Salford, and covers, under this head, the records , the parishes of Rochdale, Bury, Dean, Boltuiii Eccles and Flixton. Following on this section, we have the Hundred of Blackburn, including WhalleY' Clitheroe, Newchurch, Colne, Burnley, Rossendalef Haslingden, Padiham, ezc. The first part of the current volume completes the history of Rod:Awe', and it must be of interest to the general reader 10, observe the prominence which iS given to the cem" nection with this part of the county of the " from which the poet Byron sprung.. The fill‘i reference is to a Nicholas Byron, and 01 enough, he comes on the scene associated .10 a Warrington worthy and with the name el the street in which our own journal is published; The text runs :—" This Nicholas, who marrielt Alice, oldest daughter of Sir John Boteler, Bewsey, appears to have been the father of Sir john Byron, who had the grant tt Newstead, temp. Henry VIII." In the reiguY:l Elizabeth, Sir John Byron styles himself " Ferule' of the Manor of Rochdale." At a later peril the manor became the property of the B' family, and they took their title from it, the Peetl, lord being the sixth "Lord Byron of Rochdale' • The Byrons, do not, however, at the.present tube hold any of the Lancashire estate, the sevellth lord—the successor of the poet—having sold the' Manor of Rochdale in the year 1523. Turning to a:feature of special local interest, a° have, in the account which is given of the tun.' ship of Westhoughton, the pedigree of the "Fr' I lands" family, from which the Rylands of Viraf rington spring. We do not think it necessarY t 4) re-produce the pedigree, which is the dryest of arr reading, but we give the reference to it, which as follows : of There can be very little doubt that the fannlY Rylands was an offshoot from the parent stock of Halghton or Hulton,apd derived its patronyraicirel, the property held in (west) Halghton, a PettA;4., which retains the ancient name of "The Ryleil", i.e., the lands by the Rye or Rhee—a water-cour,seA the stream being the Cunningham Brook, wul- ' runs through a small dingle or dene. After transfer of of their lands in Westhoughton to th,./ Abbey of Cockersand, the Rylands continued reside here, holding the rank of minor gent* gentleman,tililoeu gch omn ulaonvlfl wasaDi tahi saygpealinrtil liflaoomrc sequestrationslecn, substantial yeomen. One of them, Peter Rylarroe, Rev. Peter Rylands, M.A., Trinity College, Dublin: who was educated at Winwick Grammar Scbuw* became treasurer and vicar choral of Limerick Cathl9. - dral, but died without issue in 1695, having t now and called.h is 8 0 nuWn Diana, daughter of Sir D 3 ury Wray, Bart., (a "eri tenant of Henry Cromwell's body guard in Irelatuo ; Ralph Rylands, a prosperous Westhoughton Yee: mar:: . man, who seems to have been uncle to the sego- trator, married at Dean Church, in 1613, MILL" Mather, of Winwick Parish, and settled at Culcheth. Their direct descendants for six generations ' been extensively engaged in the manufacture ° linen, sail-cloth, iron, &c., at Culcheth, Rislep Wigan, and Warrington successively (all withm about twelve miles of Westhoughton), and at the present time this branch of the fami,y is repre: sented by John Rylands, of Thel wall Grange, coui of Chester, Esq., and Thomas Glazebrook Rylsecor of Highfields, Thelwall, Esq.. elder brothers oft late Peter Rylands, 'ALP., of Massey Hall, Tbelvvallt and sous of the late John Rylands, of Bewsey Mule' Warrington. It will be seen that "Peter" is no new name in WV family, and it is not unlikely that it will re-apPar e again and again. It should be added with regard, to the volume under consideration that some the illustrations are remarkably fine. AmO:3BA the most noteworthy must be mentioned Chad's, (Rochdale), Smithell's Hall, St. Peters, (3°l' ton), Darcy Hall, Hall-We-Wood, Whalley Parish Church, Old Chapel, (Holme), and Waterfall Cliviger. Speaking for ourselves, we have a sPeciel liking for historical illustrations. They not onli help to make history intelligible—they give it life and grace.

THE resignation of Prince Bo' Bismarck's MARCK as Chancellor of GermanY Resignation. cannot be said to have been unex- pected, and yet its actual occurrence has caused sensation in Europe. He has had so much to de with the re-making of the map of Europe duriug the' last half century, and has been so thoroughly idol" tified with German interests,that Germany without BismAncK is for the moment like looking nt a body without a head. But no man is indispensable either to the world or to a nation ; and the time seems to have come when it is desirable that Ger- many should try to get along without the great German 6hancellor. It is no small thing end 31° Isingle thing that has brought about the resign!' tion. With the accession of a new Emperor there is a new order of things ; and there have been sonar),"

MOURNING ANNOUNCEMENT.

THE LAST ENEMY IS DEATH 1" The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the times of the Romans, since when it has always been popular amongst Western nations. The great mortality of this country, considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURNING. These shops, subsisting entirely on one department, are compelled to charge exorbitant prices, as many a bereaved one is able to testify, having found to her cost, when the funeral was over, that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to draw the attention of Ladies to two facts : 1— That we are manufacturers of Mantles, Costumes. and Millinery, doing a large WHOLESALE TRADE in these departments, and that we supply our customers at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. Ours being a general trade with a number of Departments,we are not dependent on our Mourning Trade for the profits,and can consequently afford to sell at Lower Prices than our competitors. Our designs are copied from the latest Paris and Berlin models, modified to suit the tastes of our various customers. Every Garment is thoroughly examined before being sent out, and for fit, finish, and style we cannot be surpassed, whilst our prices will be found nearly half of those charged elsewhere. During the Sale Special Prices will prevail in this Department. Ladies requiring deep or complimentary Mourning will receive every attention, and they will doubtless be astonished at the value which they receive.

• signs that Prince BISMARCK does not approve of the Socialistic policy which WILLIAM 11. has taken to heart. He took care not to be identified with the Rescripts which were issued on the labour question ; for he believes in crushing the Socialists rather than trying to beat them on their own ground. But the Socialists are not to be Crushed; there has just been a General Elec- tion, and they come back with an extended pro- gramme and with augmented forces. They are elected for five years, and five years of incessant struggle—even if Prince BISMARCK were allowed to have a free hand—is more than a ran readily accepts when he is close upon 75 years of age. )s`ut he is not to have a free hand; the young Emperor is making a new departure, and he is determined that his policy shall have a fair trial. It is better, therefore, that the new wine should he put into new bottles. Prince BISMARCK recog- nises this; he is getting old and weary, and he therefore retires. But "How will it end F" That is what many People are asking. The alarmists shake their heads, and say they would rather trust the old statesman than the young Emperor. There can be no question that, since the war with France, , p • ance BISMARCK has, with sound judgment and great skill, successfully exercised his powers in trying to keep Europe at peace. When a flame has shown itself, he has not fanned it— he has smothered it. The German Emperor is understood to be head-strong and warlike, and his character in this respect may be said to threaten the peace of Europe. But at the moment when the German Chancellor retires Europe is happily •••c. •-••, -free even from rumours of possible outbreak. The • • " teSignation is therefore in this respect well- " tilted. The Stock Exchange is always very sensi- tive, if not always very wise, and it is significant that it has not been affected by the news from Germany. The fact seems to be that it is gener- ellY recognised that the crisis is one which relates to the domestic rather than to the foreign politics ef the Fatherland. If the new policy is to succeed, „ it Must be carried out by men who can take their eUe from the Emperor. It may be that he is over- , I,B4oguine, as most young men are; but, even if he • ahould fail, it will be a lasting credit to him that he saw how the poor and the lowly suffered, and that he strove to better their condition. Prince ...13ISMARcK is not the man for work of this kind; he 14 a Coercionist--a powerful and consistent Coer- ' eionist, if you will; but Coercion has proved a failure in Germany, even as it has in Ireland. 1'
