The Rev. Edward Moore, of Warrington. has been the reeipient of another token of respect. This time the gift comes from the members of the Tonic Sol-fa Society which Mr. Moore has taught so successfully for several years. We echo the wish of one of the speakers who said he hoped something would turn up to save the town from losing Mr. Moore. There are many well-placed and well-paid men who could be much better spared. ,

An attempt is to be made to prohibit the intro- duction of alcoholic liquors into Central Africa; and it is to be hoped it will succeed. The three "G's" usually go together—gin, guns, and gospel •; but so far it has proved two to one against the gospel. The "civilised" native is, as a rule, a much worse creature than the African who is inno- cent cf contact with his white brother.

He was a "civilised" native was he not? who had two wives, and who was told by the good mis- sionary that he could not be regarded as a good Christian until he limited Emself to one wife. Sambo went away sorrowful; but he returned in a few days smiling and said—" Me good Christian now." "Ah, how is that?" asked the missionary. "Have you only one wife now ?" "Yes," said Sambo, "me eat the other one." Sambo had a way of his own of settling theological doubts and difficulties.

Our correspondent " Cymro " makes another appeal on behalf of the remnant of the heroes of Balaclava. He is a working-man himself, and speaks with a workman's eloquence on behalf of his class. He must be beyond shame who can read the letter in our columns without feeling that it is a disgrace to us as Englishmen to chant the praises of our heroes, and then let them die in the Work- house! We shall be glad to assist in any move- ment for aiding Donoghue,who has a special claim , upon the people of this district.

That was a terrible accident by which John Price, a workman at the Sankey Sugar Works,was killed by a passing train,on Saturday afternoon,on what is known as the Flaydock lino. It seems that the path by the line is a private one, although, by favour of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. it is much frequented as "a short cut.'; It would be very inconvenient to the residents of the district if the fatality should result in the path being closed to them. There seems to be plenty of room, if people will only keep to the path; and they take an altogether needless risk if they walk ttlong the line. , _

Dr. Richmond gave an interesting lecture on "Some Disease Germs" at a meeting, on Wednes- day evening, of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society. He startled his hearers by stating that germs are here,there and everywhere; but they were reassured on learning that of the myriads which existed in their bodies many of them were necessary for the proper fulfilment of digestive and other functions. By-the-bye, can it be that Shakespeare anticipated the germ theory when he made King Lear say— Crack Nature's moulds, all germina spill at once That make ungrateful man?

A VIOLENT NAVVY AT RUNCORN. George Hickman, a navvy, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Wednesday to answer a charge of using threats towards Mrs. Eliza Popple, of Stanley- st. The prisoner lodged at the house of Mrs. Popple, and during the past week he had been on the , " spree." On Saturday he threatened to smash her head with the poker, which he brandished aloft, and made use of most violent language. She was afraid of him.—The prisoner was bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, and he was also ordered to pay costs 15s. 2d. BICYCLES and TRICYCLES.—J. S. Garland. Warrington ; Branch. div.head: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.
div.p: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

A meeting of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League was held in St. Paul's Chambers, on Sunday, when Mr. Cox and Mr. Lindley, of Manchester, delivered addresses to a good audience. Mr. Nolan pre- sided. A letter was read from Mr. John Howlin tender- ing his resignation as president of the League, because he was unable to attend the meetings regularly. On the motion of Mr. Healey, seconded by Mr. Delaney, it was decided to ask Mr. Howlin to reconsider his decision, and retain the office of president until the expiration of his term of office. REGISTER GRATES.—L S. Garland, 51, .13 idge-street, War rington.—Advt. BREAKING A WOMAN'S LEG AT WIDNES.

„ At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Conlan, of Pear-st., was brought up on remand charged with caus- ing grievous bodily harm to Catherine Simpson, of Nelson-st. On Saturday night, the 15th February, Mrs. Simpson. a woman named Potter, and a young man named Dodd. were standing at the bar at the Royal Hotel, in Hutchinson-st., having a drink. The prisoner was also there and interrupted the conversation, and told Mrs. Simpson it was time she was at home. She told him to mind his own business, and the prisoner then seized hold of her by the shoulders, end kicked her on the left leg. She fell to the ground and when she was assisted to rise, it was discovered that the limb was broken. Dr. Hutchinson who had attended the woman, informed the magistrates that there was a wound and a slight impression in front of the leg, such as would be caused by a kick or blow. The wound could not have been caused by a fall ; there must have been direct vio- lence. The woman would not be well for another month. The prisoner, when apprehended by P.C. Thompson,said he gave the woman a push but did not kick her. He now said it was done accidentally and he was sorry the woman had met with such an accident.—He was com- mitted to take his trial at Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: REV. PETER MCKENZIE AT WIDNES.
div.p: REV. PETER MCKENZIE AT WIDNES.

...... _ This popular preacher paid a visit to Widnes on Thursday. In the afternoon he delivered a sermon to a good congregation, in Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, and in the evening he lectured, in the same place, on "Gideon, the mighty man of valour." Mr. B. Brown presided, and there was a large attendance. The pro- ceeds will be added to the circuit fund. THEATRE ROYAL RUNCORN. During the past week, the bArds of this theatre have been occupied by a capital company who have presented each night the American comedy-drama," Uncle Josh." The title-role was taken by Mr. M. Sargent Wilson, with much success, and as 'Little Tot " Miss Housley acted and sang with great ability. The piece was well staged and being full of humorous and comic situations and' dialogue the audience were kept in a constant ripple of laughter. There was withal a pathetic and tragic side to the story. " Uncle Josh " will be performed this evening.

A WIDNES TRADESMAN AND OBSTRUCTION. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, William Watts, manager of the boot shop of Messrs. Waters and Co., Waterloo-read, was summoned for obstructing the foot- path on the Bth inst. P.C. Worsfold said there were three piles of boots on the footpath in front of the defendant's shop, and about a foot from the window. Boots were also suspended from a bar about six feet high, and a number of people had to leave the footpath for fear of knocking their hats against the boots. When spoketi the defendant said he would take the boots in at night, and not beforc.—lnsrlector Keighley said he had cautioned the defandant about this practice and all shop.- keepers had had notice served upon them. —A fine of Bs. 6d. and costs was imposed. _ •

COAL ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—A FlRm's Losses. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, William Con- way, 70, Pear-street, 15 ; George Leadbetter, Water- street, 12 ; and Mirtin Wickham, 72, Pear-street, eight years of age, were each charged with stealing 2cwts. of coal, valued at Is. 6d., the property of the trustees of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.--Inspector Keighley stated that the three boys were seen by P.C. Thompsoa rolling the coal produced from a wagon on Sunday. He ran after them, and caught Conway and apprehended the other boys afterwards.—Mr. J. C. Routledge, who represented the works, said the amount of coal they lost was extremely large, being no less than frond three to four tons to week. The impudence of boys was that they would take anything they could lay their hands on.— Conlan was ordered to pay a fine of 10s., and Leadbetter and Wickham were directed to receive six strokes of the birch rod.

ALLEGED ROBBERY OF AN UMBRELLA AT RUNCORN. Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Davies at Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, Catherine Percival, a married woman of Sutherland-st , Was charged with stealing an umbrella the property of• Samuel Spann' of Bentinck-St. It appears that on Monday evening Mr. Spann's daughter, a girl about 12 years of age, went into the shop of Mr. Buck, the chemist, arid placed the um- brella she carried against the counter. On leaving she forgot the umbrella and shortly after saw Mrs. Percival who had also been in tho shop walking along the street with it. Information was given ta the police and the umbrella was found in the prisoner's house. —Mr. Smith, managing clerk to Mr. Burton, said Mr. Burton had been instructed for the defence, but he was engaged in an im- portant case at the Assizes, and wished the prisoner to be remanded until Monday. The Bench agreed and liberated the woman, who is tespectably connected on bail. UMBRELLAS, RE-COVERED at an hours' notice.--3. ,Js W. Dutton, Sankey-street. A WIDNES CHEMICAL COMPANY IN LIQUIDATION. Tin action by the overseers of Widnes against the Lancashire Allan and Sulphur Company, to recover arrears of rates amounting to £54, was again brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday.—Mr. T. J. Peters, who represented the Company, said there was no questioning the fact that the £54 was due, but a meeting of shareholders was to be held that day, when an extraordinary resolution to'wind up the concern would be passed, and a liquidator appointed. He asked for another adjournment inorder that a liquidator, might be appointed to pay the rate. There Were plenty of assets, besides £13,000 Of uncalled up capital. Mr. Peters said there was no fear of the overseers losing their money.—Mr. Timmis :If we grant a distress warrant you cannot get paid before Tuesday. Are you afraid you will lose your money.—Mr. Goff : There is a doubt about it ; we cannot be certain .—The Bench after brief consideration granted adistress warrant. ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES. The anniversary of Ireland's patron saint, St. Patrick, was observed in the usual manner at Widnes. Through- out the day large numbers of peOple were to be met wear- ing a sprig of shamrock, or a ribbon of the national colour, green. In the evening a concert was held in the Drill Hall, with a view of celebrating the event, and increasing the funds of St. Mary's Church. Prior to the commencement of the concert, the brass hind connected with the church paraded the streets of the town, and this attracted a large audience to the hall. The vocalists engaged were Miss C. Crank, soprano ; Madame Emilie Young, contralto; Mr. Sinclair, tenor; Mr. W. E. Williams, baritone ; and Messrs. T. J.-Reyes and Thos. Daniels, humourists. A capital programme was gone trough in excellent style, and the audience were not slow to show their appreciation. Selections of music were also given by the Star Handbell Ringers, and St. Mary's brass band. Miss Cullen was an efficient accom- pauist.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT RUNCORN.

In celebration of St. Patrick's Day, a concert, organised , by St. Edwards League of the Cross Brass Band, was held in the Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. A large company assembled, and were treated to an admirable entertainment. The first item on the programme was the song " Every bullet has its billet," which was rendered by Mr. A. Fox in capital style, and he was loudly applauded. Miss C. Taylor contributed "The Watchman and the Child" and "Killarney," and her well-known vocal powers were displayed to the fullest advantage; Miss Stubbs sung " Caris'sima " and "Kathleen Mavourneen" and created a good impression by her powerful and tundul rendering. Theappropriate song "The Wearing of the Green "was rendered by Mr. T. Clegg, who Lad added a verse of his own composition,- hi which Mr. Gladstone's name found a place, Mr. Clegg was treated to a tremendous oration, and responded in the usual manner to unanimous encores. A couple of songs were given by Mr. J. Moran, of Widnes, and his clever step dancing was a feature of the entertainment and the audience Would not be satisfied without a repetition. Mr. H. Pilgrim sang " Madeline" and "Good Company " ; Mr. W. Edwardson, "Alice, where art thou"; and Mr. Starkey " Homeward, once more" and" The Old Mud Cabin " ; all of whom met with merited success. Mr. James Wood,a local instrumentall it of repute, performed the cornet solos, " The Conquer- ing Hero," and "Killarney,". with fine effect, and ,received the hearty plaudits of thos3 present. Mr. J. Ravenscroft ably officiated as:accompanist to the Various vocalists. In the course of the evening the League of the cross played several selections of music and the " Run- corn Prize Quartette Party" also contributed a vocal selection with success.

BASINETTES, new designs.—Gerland, Ironmonger, War- rington.—Adrt. COUNTERFEIT SOVEREIGNS_ AT RUNCORN.

There are at present in circulation a number of base sovereigns which are so admirable a counter- feit of the real coin that detection is rendered difficult and tradesmen would do well to exercise more than ordinary care. The base coin cannot be distinguished from the genuine by colour or appear- ance; is of the exact standyd weight, and with- stands the acid test. The nose of the head is, however, of a more Roman character than that which adorns the genuine sovereign and the "a "in Victoria is out of line.

THE SUBSIDENCES /N CHESHIEE. At the Northwich Local Board meeting, en Wed- nesday, on the question of the opposition to bo given to the Widnes Brine Bill coming up for dis- cussion, it was stated that Professor Boyd Dawkins, of Manebeger, had visited Northwich on the pre- vious Saturday, and had inspected the town, as well as the site of the proposed pumping station at Wincham, with a view of giving a report to the parliamentary committee. The result so far had been highly satisfactory, and the committee con- sidered that the report would prove not only of great value so far as concerned the opposition to the Widnes Bill, but also on the general question of subsidence. It was reported that the Bill would not be before the committee until the end of April or the beginning of May. At the same meeting, on the motion of Mr. Maddecks, it was resolved to for- ward all details on the subsidence qnestion to mem- bers of Parliament and to the President of the Local Government Board; and to ask Mr. Ritchie to grant a Royal Commission to inquire fully into the subject. ALARMING GAS EXPLOSION AT ST. HELENS: A HOUSE WRECKED.

An alarming explosion of gas, which occasioned considerable destruction occurred at 52 Bickerstaff- ate St. Helens, the residence of Mr. Alfred Turley, picture dealer-and house furnisher, on Wednesday night. About half-past seven Miss Jessie Turley entered the parlour and struck a match with the intention of lightinbthe gas. Immediately she did so a tremendous report was heard for some hundreds of yards around,and the adjoining houses were shaken in an alarming manner. Crowds flocked to the spot and it was found that the explosion of gas—for such it proved to be—had consequences of a serious nature. The parlour was completely wrecked, the door shattered am/ the windows were blown bodily into the street--the glass smashing against the wall of Messrs. Greenall's brewery on the, opposite side. The brick wall facing the parlour door was blown down,and fell into the entry leading to the back of the premises, while upstairs and downstairs nearly every window was smashed, and the walls and ceilings damaged and cracked. Pictures and other articles were destroyed by the flame, and the escap- inggas from the top_ ...of the chandelier becoming ignited, was the (=anon- for sending for the fire brigade. The brigade quickly arrived, and their services were valuable at the moment. Miss Turley had her face burnt while the whole ot her hair was badly singed. A younger brother, named Harold, was also singed and burned about the head. The other occupants of the house had an almost miracu- lous escape from injury, considering the great des- truction of property. The damage is estimated at about £l5O.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. There is every prospect of a keen contest in the election of five members to the Local Board, which is fixed to be decided on April Ist. The candidates of the Owners' and Occupiers' Association and also their four opponents have issued addresses to the ratepayers. setting forth their claims.: Two public meetings have been held during the past week in support of Messrs. Hargreaves. Neil, Beech, and Tilley, but the attendance ot the public has been very meagre on each occasion, and the battle will have obe won, as usual, by canvassing. Beyond issuing an address, Messrs. Gossage, Carey, Handley, Sadler and Owens, have made no move to secure their return, but the votes of the manufacturing interest is assured, and their seats may be .consi- dered comparatively safe.

• • -- The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. T. S. Timmins presided, and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, Messrs. R. H. Davies, H. W. Deacon, C. Barlow, B. Brown, S. Quinn, and G. H. Danby, olerk. TEE CLERICS SALARY. The General Purposes Committee reported that they had received the report and recommendation of the Finance Committee and it was resolved that the report , be adopted so far as the junior clerk was concerned—that his salary be advanced by Ll 5 per annum .—Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption cai the minutes.—Major War•ing said the Finance Committee intended their recommend- ation to be brought before the Board, and he moved that it be now presented to the Board.—Dean Finegan seconded the motion,which was carried.—The Clerk then read the report, which gave some details of the clerks work and recommeqed that his salary be advanced from £3OO to £4OO a year.—Major Wareing proposed that this recommendation be approved and adopted—Mr. Barlow seconded, because he thought the matter should come before the Board.—Dean Finegan opposed the motion because he did not think the clerk was badly paid at his present remuneration. He questioned the wisdom of discussing the report at present, as assertions were made as to the savings effected by the clerk, which he was not prepared to • accept, and .the meMbern of the Board had not had an opportunity to ascertain if they were correct. The speaker alleged that the report was not the report of the Finance Committee, but had been ,drawn out and written by Mr. Danby himself, and he complained that notice thot this question would be brought up was not given to the members of the Finance Committee.—Mr. Deacon said the Clerk's claim of the credit of carrying out the scheme for the conversion of the loans, by which a considerable saving was effected, was ridiculous on the face of it.. He was of opinion that the Clerk had been fully paid for his services in the past, and that it would be unwise to increase the salary.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the Clerk certainly had a great deal of trouble in the con- solidation of the loans, in the way of making out statis- tics, dtc.—The Chairman said the Board thought it their duty to pay a servant liberally, and he believed that Mr. Danby 7as paid sufficiently lileral salary for his post. With regard to the junior Clerk, he was entitled to an in- crease of salary.—agaiust the proppsed addition to the Clerk's salary there voted the Chairman, Dean Finegan Father Clark, Mr. Deacon, a,nd Mr. Quinn-5. The other members abstained from voting, and the proposal was therefore lost. The recommendation as to the junior Clerk was adopted unanimously.

DISTRICT EDUCATION. The District Education Committee reported that dur.: ing February there were 106 applications for school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 91 cases. 213 parents were summoned before the Committee for con- travention of the Education Act, and 32 were prosecuted before the rnagistates and convicted. Major Wareing asked if it was the custom of the District Education Committee to require doctor's certificates in all cases of where children were not attending school through sick- ness, and were the parents of such children required to pay for the certificate.—Mr. Deacon said the Committee did not require certificates in all cases. If the Com- mittee demanded a certificate the parent had to pay for it. He explained that the Committee exercised the greatest care in these cases, and had no desire to deal harshly with parents, and never asked for a certificate if they were satisfied it was a hona fide case of sickness. A certificate could be obta,:ned for 3d., which was not a large outlay, and to some of these certificates the Com- mittee paid great deference and others they viewed with a little distrust. (Laughter.) Dean Finegan pointed out that the Prescot Uhion had passed a law that in the case of poor parents, the children should be sent to a local doctor, and the certificate paid for by the Union. This law was for the school attendance district, but he did not see why it should not be extended to Widnes.— Mr. Deacon promised to look into the matter.

NEW STANDING ORDER. , Dean Finegan moved " that when the question of an ' increase of salary to any officer or ser:ant of the Board is considered at any committee meeting, notice of the proposed increase he entered upon the summonses 'sent --to each member of .the Committee." He pointed out that this was not done in the case of Mr. Danbv's pro- posed increase and he had never known such an omis- sion to take place when it was to increase the salary of a pupil teacher or the wages of a caretaker. This resolu- tion would prevent the Clerk committing that error again.—Fatner Clark seconded—The Chairman, said he did not believe that the Clerk purposely omitted the information from the agenda paper. (Hear, hear). It was quite right that members should know what was coming on before thy went to a meeting.—Dean Finegan: That is all I want.—The motion was carried unanimously and was added to the standing orders.
RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE PUBLIC MEETING.

Jo. connection with the Runcorn branch of the Sons of TeMperance, a public meeting was held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Monday evening. There was a moderate attendance. Mr. P. J. Nor- man presided, and was supported on the platform by the Rev. H. Burson (Wesleyan superintendent),

Rev. A. H. Sanderson (curate, Holy Trinity Church), Messrs. W. Huddart, M.W.P.. of Manchester ; D. Bis- brown, and T. Cooke (secretary). A hymn having bean sung, the Rev. A. H. Sanderson offered up prayer. The Rev. H. Burson, who had to attend another engagement, addressed the meeting. He said he was there to express sympathy with this work, and what was more, if a Wes- leyan minister's blessing was worth anything, he gave them his benediction, and he said "God speed the Sons of Temperance." This organisation had an additional claim upon them, because in addition to circulating the good and true principles of total abstinence, it also en- couraged the spirit of thrift and economy and of self- help. This was a benefit to society, and taught the mem- bers to look out for a rainy day. Total abstinence was a fortification against many of the ills of life ; they were shielded from many ordinary daily calamities ; still thr. had their rainy day ; and they were taught to anticipate that day. They did not believe in calling in the relieving officer, or seeking aid from the Board of Guardians. They believed in calling in the secretary of an institu- tion like that; in other words, they believed in helping themselves. (Applause.) The Chairman, in the course of a brief speech, said every research of modern science and every new experi- ment of the medical profession, strengthened the fun- damental arguments they had in favour of the fact that total abstinence was the best thing for man from 'every standpoint. (Applause.) Alluding to the poor attend- mice, the Chairman pointed out the League of the Cross were celebrating St. Patricks day, at the Public Hall, and if that celebration had taken away some members they were not jealous, because the League of the Cross was endeavoung to extend the principles of total abstin- ence. They were glad to think that St. Patrick's Day that used to be celebrated in such different style was now being celebrated with the direct object of makint people teetotal. tApplause.) The primary object of the Committee of the Sons of Temperance in holding that meeting was to make everybody teetotal, and the second object was to make them sons of temperance. They not only wanted to make people to be teetotal but also to be thrifty. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman quoted statistics of an assurance society to show that the percentage of deaths amongst the teetotal section was much less than in the non-teetotal section' and he contended that on all grounds people would find it to pay to be teetotal. (Applause.) The Per. A. H. Sanderson said, like Mr. Burson, he was present to show his sympathy with the object of the society, and said his only recommendation was that be was a total abstainer of nearly 15 years standing. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Huddart then delivered an address on the principles and benefit of the Sons of Temperance, and said before a person could become a member he must be a tctal abstainer, and if he desired to remain a member he must remain a total abstainer. By joining the local lodge they became members of the Cheshire Grand Divi- sion. The speaker stated that the society had met all the lcgitimate claims that were made upon it, and its proud boast was that they had paid 20s. in the pound, and with the present systeniof financing they had a pros- pect of doing it far easier in the future than they had done in the past. (Applause.) In the Cheshire Grand Division if sickness overtook its members, instead of pay- ing the sick member.; 103, for 26 weeks, which was the long,-at period Friendly Societies gave it, the Sons of Temperance gave 10. s. per week for 12 months. (Ap- plause.) If the sickness should continue, the Order of Oddfellows would give a member perhaps half the pay- ment for another 26 weeks, whilst the Sons of Temper- ance would give its member half benefit for another 12 months. (Applause.) In the Friendly Societies; if a member continue to be sick, there was a system of buy- ing them out by giving a certain sum of money, but the Sons of Temperance paid one-quarter of the benefit as long as sickness continued. (Hear, hear.) Where could they find any ozder which held its mild-lags at a public- house that could show such generosity as that? He thought they would have a difficulty in doing so. The reason was that the sick and dos.th-rate of the Sons of Temperance was less than it was amongst other so.iet lee, The speaker then dealt with the/general aspect of the temperance question in forcible terms.—Mr. T. Cooke proposed a vote of thanks -to the Chairman and the ! speakers in a liumourous speech, and the motion being seconded bytir. Bisbrown9 was carried by acclamation, and the meeting closed with the siughie ( a the Doxology, In the course of the proceedings the audience sang a number Of hymns in hearty style ; Mr. Wesley Cooke accompanying , on the harmonium.

THE EXTENSION OF BOROUGIkS

During the proceedings of the Parli;Lmentary Committee of the Lancashire Council at their meet- ing at Preston, on Monday, a comtmlnicitlon by the Local Government Board of their tlects:i:nr net to approve an exelJnsion of municipal area at flattop, was read by Mr. Button, Clerk of the County Council. —Mr. Briezley complained of the Litrairness to parishes, proposed to b, included, in Ihe inat ter of costs. He knew that in one parish a rate of six- pence in t he pound hint been wade nece.ssary to meet the cost the inhabitants were out in their opposi- tion to the Bolton application. With a view to the subject being considered by the County Council, he moved a ,resolution to ask the Local Government ' Board to allow costs in such eascg.—Mr. J. C. Sutton said that upon extract from the evidence and speeches at the Bolton Inquiry of their material substance it would be seen by how simple and inexpensive a process the merits couid have been grasped- and the Local Govern- ment Board have been guided to' the 'conclusion they had arrived at. The fact that out of the many thous- ands of pounds expended, absolutely nothing remained, to any one of the parties to the Inquiry; except a heap of waste paper, was one deeply to be deplored. He fully agreed with Mr. Brierley's observations, but, as no statu- tory powers were possessed by the Local Government Board. legislation thereon was needed, and he would prefer a petition by the Council to Parliament, and a request to an influential county member to support it.— Mr, F. A. Roberts and several members of the Committee thought the motion of Mr. Brierley woula lead to new legislation on the subject.—The Rev. Canon Royds asked in 'What proportions the costs fell upon parties. —Mr. Ji. C. Sutton said he thought the costs of the Bolton Mund cipal and Rural Authorities would approach £5,000, an- he estimated that, inclusive of £750 by the county, the total cost of the opponents would approach a similar fund.—Mr. Brierley's motion was unanimously • adopted. BOROUGH BILLS IN PARLIAMENT.

The preaiding Chairman (Mr. V. K. Armitage) said the agenda included a request by Mr. Hutton for the appoint- ment of a sub-committee of members of the Parliamentary Committee with a view to arranging for the attendance of members during proceedings in which the county is interested. Mr. Flulton had explained to him the desirable- ness of the council being so represented. Mr. Sutton had also just now pointed out that, as prompt decisions are often required in connection with important prop.- sals, the responsibility of their rejection or acceptance should not rest upon the Clerk of the Council. He (the Chairman) thought that these circumstances called for the appointment of such a cominittee.—Mr. Sutton said he would move that the Right Hon. J. T. Ilibbert, chair- man of the Council, Mr. Charles R. Jacson, vice-chair- man of the Council, as members of the Parliamentary Committee, and Mr. Maskell Peace, chairman, and Mr. V. K. Armitage, vice-chairman of the Committee, form part of the sub-Committee with a view to two of the number being present at Westminster when circum- stances made it desirable for Mr. Hulton so to arrange; and, in view of the Bills before Parliament, he would move that Dr. Fitzpatrick, Mr. Brierley, and Mr. Beardoe Grundy be added with the intention that one of them be also present.—Mr. Travers Hayes moved, and Mr. Isher- wood seconded, a proposal to add the name of Mr. J. C. Sutton, and the Committee was appointed accordingly.

div.head: MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.
div.p: MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.

A meeting of the members of the Conservative party in both Houses of Parliament, was held at the Carlton Club, London, 'at noon, on Thursday. Amongst those present were—Mr. Smith, Mr. Balfour, Mr. Goschen, Mr. Matthews, Mr. Stanhope; Lords Ravensworth, Wey- mouth, Grirnston, Rowton, Curzon, Pembroke, and Cran- brook ; the Marquis of Granby, Sir A. Rollit, Mr. Ash- mead-Bartlett, Sir Richard Temple, Lord Knutsford, Lord Lathom, Viscount Cranborne, Lord liming, Capt. Selwyn, the Duke of Portland, the Duke of Rut- land, Lord Ashbourne, Baron de Worms, Mr. Jackson, Lord Dunraven, Lord George Hamilton, Mr. Ritchie, Lord Colville of Culross, Marquess of Carmarthen, Lord Brownlow. Viscount Lewisham, and Mr. Raikm Lord Salisbury, on rising to address the meeting, was received with great cheering. He enjoined upon those present that the proceedings should be regarded as private, and explained that the meeting had been called in redemp- tion of a pledge that more freouent opportunities should ' be afforded for the exchange of opinion on topics of' the , day between the leaders and the rank and file. Matters over which he had no control had prevented him from calling the meeting earlier. His lordship referred to the Tithes Bill and the Land Purchase Bill, and pointed out that there should not be undue discussion on either of these Rills. There would probably be obstruction from the other side, but it was in the highest degree desirable that the Conservative party should work to- gether. There had been much talk recently about an immediate dissolution ; but gossip of that kind should be taken for what it was worth. The Government were doing good work, and he believed they retained the loyal support of the country. The time for the general election was, however, drawing near, and organization in constituencies should be pertected. He hoped every member would be able to make an effort to be unremitt- ing in his attendance in the House, and give constant and undivided support to the Government throughout the session. Some discussion ensued on the Tithes Bill and foreign policy. The meeting, which lasted over an hour, was of the most amicable character. WARRINGTON BANKRUPTC Y COURT.
A sitting of this Court was held yesterday, before the Registrar (Captain Nicholson), the examinations being conducted by the Official Receiver, Mr. C. .1. Dibb.

Ties EXAMINATION of John Woolstencroft, lately carry- ing on business as a stationer, in Horsemarket-st., was declared closed, the requirements of the Court having been complied with. FAILURE OF A RUNCORN SHOEMAXER.—Joseph boot and shoemaker, 56, High-st., Runcorn, came up for , his first examination. A receiving order was made against the debtor on his own petition, and he was ad- judged bankrupt on the sth inst. In his statement to tke Official Receiver bankrupt states that about seven yes.rs ago he entered into partnership with his father, James Mclninn, wto carried on the business of a boot and shoemaker, at 56, High-st., Runcorn. They ' traded under the style of James Mclninn and Son. Debtor had no capital. The business then , showed a surplus of about £2OO, without allowing ' for depreciation. In September, 1887, his father went to live in Scotland, and bankrupt entered into an agreement to pay him 15s. a week for the rest of his life, besides the premium on his insurance policy (abeut , £2O per annum), and the interest on the mortgage of hiahouse, 56, High-street, amounting to £2O per annum. On May 20th, 1889, debtor executed a deed of assign- ment for the benefit of his creditors, in favour of J. W. I Lamb, of 72, Lil-street, Manchester. His father was also forced to execute the deed on the ground that he was a partner. Mr. Lamb sold the business to Mr. Irving, who sold it to bankrupt's wife; and she now carried on the shoemaking business, bankrupt being her manoger. Mr. Lamb realised about £240 by the sale of the stock, and the equity of the house, land collected about £5O from book debts. He had paid a dividend of 6s. 9d. in the £ to the joint credi- tors. Debtor had no separate assets. He explained his deficiency by bad tratte, and by reason of his expenses being greater than his profits. He had resorted to the Bankruptcy Court in consequence of one of his creditors having caused him to be served with a bankruptcy notice. With regard to the latter creditor, he said: " I became surety for £4O borrowed by George Hunt, my father-in-law, from J. F. Townend. I received £2O of the amount. I have since been sued by Townend for £5O lie. Bd., and Hunt became bankrupt last year." After debtor had been Questioned by the Official Becziver, the examination was adjourned until May 2nd. A PROVISION DEALER'S AFFAIRS.—Thomas Higgins provision dealer, 18, Stepheu-st., Manchester-road, War- rington, attended to undergo his first examination. Bankrupt in his statement to the Official Receiver, says that up to 1882 he was a coachman and gardener. In October, 1882, he commenced business as a provision dealer, at him, and in 1883 took a shop, No. 47, Church- at., Warrington. Subsequently he removed to Man- chester-road, and only had a stall in the market. When he commenced business he had five cottages in Ireland, which he afterwards sold for £llO. In explanation of the deficiency of £l9l 14s. 11d., debtor put down £l3O Bs. 4d. as representing losS in business through mis- management of his wife and step-daughter during his absence when selling with his cart.—The examination was adjourned.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
AN UNRULY RAILWAY PASSIM:IER AT .NEWTON.

--- Anthony McNamara, described as a tailor, of Liver- pool, was brought up in custody at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, en Wednesday, on charges of having, on the 18th inst., obstructed the servants of the London and North-Western Railway Company, at New- ton Station, and of having wilfully broken a window at the station. He had to be ejected from the station pre- snises and afterwards smashedavrindow. For obstruct- ing the railway servants he was fined 55., and 7s. costs, and for the damage a fine of 55., and 2s. 6d. costs, waif imposed, the alternative of non-payment being 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: IN CONFLICT wrm nog Poucs.
div.p: IN CONFLICT wrm nog Poucs.

Bridget Costello (30), of Ship-yard, was before the magistrates on Tuesday, on a charge of drunkenness and assault. It was alleged that as Constable Clough was taking a man into custody on Monday evening, prisoner, who was drunk, struck him a violent blow on the mouth. She was punished for the offence by being sent to prison for a fortnight, with hard labour. At the same sitting of the Court, a youth named. Patrick Thompson, a forge- hand, living in Stamford-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fennel-st. on the previous even- ing, and with assaulting Constables Evans and Wade. He also was curunitted to gaol for 14 days, with hard labour.

div.head: AN OEJNCTION TO A FATHER-IN-LAW.
div.p: AN OEJNCTION TO A FATHER-IN-LAW.

John Tiale,-SraTe;,-lioge-r-st.,was charged at the War- rington Police Court, on Tuesday, with having on Sunday assaulted and beaten his wife. Complainant said on Sunday her husband kicked arid " punched " her. He told her to leave the house. She did so, and when she returned he was breaking the windows—Defendant: It is all on account of her father-in-law. If she will promise to part with him we should be comfortable.— Complainant: I will not do so.—Defendant : I have never had any comfort since her father-in-law came into the house.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six mouths, in the sum of £5, or go to prison for 14 days.
THE- CHIEF CONSTABLE POURS OIL ON THE TROUBLED
Went as .

On Tuesday. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable of War- rington, acted as mediator between a married couple who came to the Police Court to have their differences inquired into. The husband, a forge hand named Nester, was defendant, and was charged by his wife with having assaulted her on the 17th inst. Complainant said her husband had struck her and pushed her against the wall. In reply to the Chief Constable, she at first said that she could not forgive her husband, but after some persuasion the complainant and defendant, accompanied by a police- man, left the room with the object of endeavouring to settle the quarrel. At the conclusion of the other busi- ness before the Court it was announced that the two had agreed to live together again, and the case was, therefore, dismissed upon the defendant paying the cost of tha warrant, ss. A Lo WHO WISHED TOOO TO THIS " CLIO."

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, a man named Bark was summoned for not regularly sending his stepson, Wilifam Dews, to school. Mr. Riley said that this was a case which had been within the knowledge of the Committee far a long time; but no proceedings had been taken because the step-father was not to blame for the lad's non-attendance at school. He was satis- fied he had done the best he could for him. The lad had net only played truant, but frequently absented himself from home for days together, and no one knew where he had been sleeping nor how he had obtained food. He was eleven years and six months old, and should be put under constraint. He (Mr. Riley) had been instructed to ask for the lad to 14, sent to the training ship Clio. The Clerk asked the lad if he was willing to go to the ship, and if he ran away from home on purpose to be sent away? Dews replied in the affirmative to both questions, and the magistrates decided to accede to the request and ordered that he be sent to the Clio.

div.head: RUNNING AGAINST A HEN.
div.p: RUNNING AGAINST A HEN.

Arthur Henry Rowlands, James Grady, Patrick Grady, Alfred Ford, and Joseph Allen, all young lads, appeared at Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, on a charge ef stealing a hen the property of John Welsby, of Brick-st. About half past nine on the previous night P.C. Bolling- ' worth was pa,nsing Mrs. Locker's shop in Mill-st. when he saw the lads Rowlands and James Grady attempting to sell a hen. He questioned Rowlands as to where he had got the hen and the lad told him he had been sent to sell it by his father who was out of work and in want of bread. The officer was not satisfied with this pathetic tale, and on telling Rowlands he would have to go to the police station, the latter admitted that the hen was Mr. Welsby's and made a statement which implicated the other lads. When Ford was arrested he told the officer that they were playing " henning" in Mr. Welshy's yard and he ran against the hen which was sitting on a rail and they took it. The lads having been locked up over night, the bench now discharged them with a caution to do better in the future.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATITEDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Councillor

Voisey. DRUNKENNESS. —William Higham, for having been drunk in Liverpool-road on the previous night, was fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days. STEALING CHEESE.— Walter Warburton, labourer, who lives in Winwick-st., appeared in the dock on a charge of having stolen three pounds of cheese belonging to Miss Kendrick, of Wilderspool-road. It appeared that on Friday afternoon prisoner went begging to Miss Ken- drick's house. He was refused alms, and soon after he had gone the cheese was missed from a meat safe in the yard. P.C. Wade was put on prisoner's track, but the latter, as soon as the officer attempted to arrest him, threw the cheese into the river. Some bread dropped out of his pocket at the same time. Prisoner now alleged that a man had given him the cheese.—The Magistrate's Clerk: And the bread too ?—Prisoner: Yes. —Magistrate's Clerk: Did he not offer you a glass of beer at the same time? (Laughter.)—Prisoner: No.— Alderman Burgess said it was not the first time prisoner had been before the court for appropriating otherpeople's goods. He would be fined 20s. and costs, or in default a months' imprisonment. MONDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Sutton. DRUNICENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Richard Whittaker, Buttermarket- street, Saturday night, fined ss. including costs ; Joseph Warburton, Winwick-street, Saturday night, fined 10s. and costs; Martin Dolan, Town-hill, Saturday night, fined ss. and costs ; Edward Smith, Church-street, Sun- day night, discharged with a caution; and Mary Mit- chell, Friar's-green, 11th March, fined ss. and costs. ALLEGED ROBBERY.—Edward Sauce, a labourer, was charged with having on Sunday night stolen a cap be- longing to Thomas Williams. Prosecutor, who is a navvy employed on the Ship Canal, seemed reluctant to give evidence against the accused, whom the Bench iischarged. BYE-LAW OFFENCES.—Margaret Galvin, a lodging- house keeper, Ship-yard, was summoned for having neg- lected to have the walls, ceilings, Sm.' of her house whitewashed, and the floor swept regularly. She was ordered to pay the costs. CHIMNEYS ON Fiee.—Peter Cotton, Chester's-yard, and Henry Gittens, Swan Inn, Bridge-street, were each ordered to pay a fine of is. for having allowed the chimneys of their dwelling-houses to be on fire.—For a similar offence, Ellen Butterworth, Rain's Head, Horse- market-street, was fined Is. and costs. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—James Leonardy, a boy, was summoned for having wheeled a coal wagon on the footpath in Winwick-street, to the obstruction of passen- gers, on the 11th March. He was fined in the costs &. WINDOW Slum/co.—John Conway, Dial-court, pleaded guilty to having been drunk and disorderly in Dial- court, on Saturday night, and to having wilfully broken five panes of glass ma house in the same court. Pri- soner got drunk and went to his father's house and created a disturbance. On being remonstrated with, he hurled several stones through the window. Afine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, was imposed. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest and C. M. Crosfield. _ _ .

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches rlayed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

HOLY CROSS GUILD (ST. HELENS) V. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.—PIayed at St. Helens on Saturday. The home team played thirteen men. Final result: Parish Church 2 goals, 2 tries, 1 minor; Guild: 1 try 7 minors. RUNCORN " V. WIGAN " a."—Saturday saw these teams engaged at Runcorn to try conclusions. No score was made during the first part of the game; but in the second half Hollingworth, made a dashing run, and Pendlebury receiving the ball, secured a try, and later on Robinson crossed the line. Runcorn's score was 2 tries, 2 minors ; Wigan, nil.

WARRINGTON ST. ELPRIN'S V. WYCLIFFB.—These junior organizations met for the first time this season on the ground of the latter on Saturday afternoon. Both sides weie strongly represented, and the home team winning the toss, they elected to play with the wind in their favour. The visitors kicked off, and the play was for some time of a very even nature. The oval was gradu- ally worked down to the visitors' line, and, from a line- out. Noon dodged over and grounded at the corner flag. Cartwright took the difficult place, and kicked a magni- ficent goal. The visitors after this reverse seemed to play up with renewed energy, and some severe and pro- tracted scrimmages took place on the home line. Brundritt, however, eventually relieved by a good run to the home 25. Wycliffe subsequently pressed, and a minor was conceded, the score at half-time being— Wycliffe, a goal and a minor to nil. St. Elphin's soon after the re-start played up very pluckily, and their efforts were at length rewarded by a try, which was converted into a goal. They subsequently obtained a minor. As the scores were now equal, each side strove to obtain the winning point. This was eventually ob- tained by Hampson scoring for Wycliffe after a combined rush of the forwards. Cartwright failed at the place. Nothing further was scored, and a pleasant and exciting game ended in a win for Wycliffe by a try. Score : Wycliffe, 1 gaol, 1 try, 1 minor; St. Elphin's, 1 goal, 1 minor. On behalf of Wycliffe, Brunclritt, Beaman, Noon, Cartwright, and Bickerstaffe played a very good game. RTJNCORN V. LEEDS Sr. Joss's.—For the second time this season these teams met on Saturday, the return match being Played off at Leeds. When the teams met early on in the season for the first time, the Saints, were thoroughly defeated by the cracks of Cheshire, being niled, whilst Runcorn's score was four goals. The Run- corn team comprised: Houghton (back), Davies, Cromp- ton, and Abrams (three-quarter backs) ; Evans and Hughes (half backs) ; Huglses,Dolan, Hancock, Faulkner' Gayter, Riley, Hampson' Broady and Rigby (forwards). Hughes, for Runcorn, kicked off, and the visitors' quarters were at once attacked. Relief, however, was given by Potter, who returned well into touch, Runcorn being compelled to touch down. Faulkner soon after- wards obtained possession of the ball, and made for the visitors citadel; but Hepper haying a free kick conceded essayed to improve matters ; but the ball was kicked dead. The game pros c,eeded most evenly for a time until a pass was given by Riley to Hancock, who scored the first try for Runcorn, Floughton, who made a good effort to improve matters, failed at goal. Leeds kicked off. On the drop- out, a splendid rush was made, and to save Davies touched down. Then the home team succeeded in get- ting over the line; but the attempt at goal was a failure. Eventually the Cheshire men broke away, and Faulkner secured a try, which was converted into a goal by Crompton. This brought up half time, with the score: Runcorn,l goal, 1 try ; Leeds/St. John's, 1 try and 5 minors. After the usual interval, the game was recom- menced by the home team. Crompton was in good form, and, watching his opportunity, soon got over, and planted the second goal for his team. This was a fine performance, and he was cheered for his display. Pres- sure was then put upon the Cheshire men, but this was only of short duration, as Davies secured possession, and made one of those runs which have made him famous, ending in registering a try after traversing three parts the length of the field. Crompton did the needful, adding the third goal, and after some even, and at the same time, exciting play, the latter player crossed the line, and added a fourth goal. At the conclusion Runcorn were the winners of the game, having scored four goals and one try, whilst St. John's score was one try and nine minors. WIDNES V. CROMPTON.—These clubs met at Widnes on Saturday afternoon before a large number of spectators. Hill started the ball for the visitors, but no return was made. The ball was gradually worked opposite the home goal, where a penalty kick was awarded to Widnes. Some good passing by Mills and Howarth placed the home line in danger, but Brennan brought relief by a good run and kick to neutral territory. Clarke got pos- session from McGurl, but was thrown in touch in attempting to evade the visitors' full back. Play was subsequently transferred to the home quarter by Clough, but he was collared by Clarke .and Brennan. Butter- worth and Groves were next conspicuous with some good forward play, while the passing of Walsh and Mills was neutralized by the efforts of Peters. Stubbs next headed a.good dribble, and from a series of scrimmages on the visitors' line, McGurl got over and registered a try, amidst cheers. Gordon took the place kick, which failed. From the drop out the visitors invaded the home quarter, where Clough made a futile attempt at goal. Following up the ball, the visitors compelled Clarke to touch down. McGurl from a scrimmage gave Brennan

a pass, and he dropped a neat goal. At Flail time the score was'Widnes one goal, one try, and one minor; to Crompton one minor. On changing ends the home team again assumed the aggressive. and Farrell, who got possession in the visitor's quarter, after a splendid run registered the second try. The place kick, however, failed. The success on the part of the home team seemed to irritate the visitors, who next compelled their oppon- ents to beat a hasty retreat, Hill, Stott, and Jones being mainly responsible for this. Stott subsequently got over, and placed the ball behind theposts, from which an easy goal was kicked. The home team next pressed, and a minor resulted in their favour. Stott again crossed the home line, but the attempt at goal failed. Howarth next made a good run for the visitors, but just before crossing the line he was brought down by Clarke. Clough was similarly treated by Hartles. The home team was awarded a penalty kick, from which Holt made a splendid run from the centre and crossed the line midst enthusiastic cheers. Farrell supplemented his efforts by sending the leather between the uprights. A well contested game ended in a win for Widnes by two goals, two tries, and two minors to Crompton one goal, one try, and two minors. Teams :—Widnes; Hartles, fullback ; Peters, Brennan, and Clarke, three-quarters: Farrell and McGurl, half tacks ; Smith, Pearson, Farmer, Gandy, Holt, Stubbs, Whelan, Gordon, and Toilkies, forwards. Crompton: Jones, full back; Howarth, Clough, Stott, three-quarters backs; Hill and Mills, half backs; Groves, *Wolstencroft. Butterworth, Wild, Whittaker, Walsh, Winterbottom, Sucksmith, and Wood, forwards. Referee, Mr. Williamson. WARRINGTON " A " V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERBRS.—The Warringtonians journFiyed to Birkenhead to fulfil this return fixture on Saturday, a large number of spectators assembling to witness the game. The visitors winning the toss, Garner for the home team started against a . . . . .

stiffish breeze, and no return being forthcomin-g, play settled near the visitors' lines. Sampson, however, was the chief operator in getting the ball to neutral territory by a good kick, and Davies and Molyneux, by some rare good tackling, enabling the visiting forwards to dribble over the line, Watson running the ball out rather riskily. From the succeeding line out the ball was rushed over, Bate being the lucky one to score. From the drop out play waged very fast. Jolley and Thornlev transferred the game to their opponents' quarters, and the former fiioring Watson enabled the visitors to rush bodily under the posts, where Williams, securing from a pack, threw grandly across to Sampson, who scored a try, Jolley kick- ing a grand goal. Thornley charged the kick off, but Hurst got the ball cleverly away. Following a series of free kicks Rowe, from a pass by Williams, got a clear field, and mainly through his efforts the home tirim were pressed, and Nosworthy making a sad mess of a free kick, enabled Molyneux to secure another try. The visitors now played up strongly, Davies, Isherwood, and ' Barnes doing some good work. Jolley and Herbert for their respective sides put in some good runs, Warrington in the end being forced to defend. The home forwards were now playing very strongly, and tried every effort 4 to score, but without avail, for some sterling work by Davies, Isherwood, and Barnes staved off the threatened danger, and some passing among the home backs failing to come off, the ball was rushed to midfield. Speakman was next loudly cheered for a grand piece of play along touch, but this was responded to by Herbert getting away from a pack and passing to Watson, who was, quickly tackled. The ball, however, got loose, and some unaccountable mulling amongst the visiting backs ended in the ball being kicked over the line, and Kelly rushing up secured a try, half-time being called with Warrington 1-2 to 0-1-0. Restarting, the Wanderers were soon forced to defend, but after once clearing their lines they eot clear away to the opposite end of the field, with the result that Boscow was tackled in close proximity to the
Same

line. The defence was too good at this period, and I Thornley effected a capital relief by a strong rush, and kicked beyond the centre line. Atter Jolley had repeatedly checked Watson, Speakman got a pretty try from a pass by Williams, which was for some unknown reason disallowed. Immediately afterwards, however, Rowe secured from a pack, and after feigning to pass fairly outwitted his opponents, and got the best try of the match, under the posts, Jolley kicking a goal. Soon after the drop out the whistle was blown for some in- formality, but the home players keeping on, Herbert got a try, which was allowed. After the drop out Nelson effected a cross dribble, but Boscow just saved. Rowe and Jolley by a couple of strong runs, transferred the oval to the opposite end of the ground, and after some fine exchange kicks, Russell got away with a good drib- ble. The game was now being fiercely contested in the Wanderer's quarters, and Rowe almost dropped a goal, the ball being blown outside the posts, a minor resulting. Some capital passing was next witnessed between Isherwood, Russell, Jolley, and Sampson, but only a minor was given. The ball was eventually worked to the visitor's line, and Atkinson secured the last try, the final score being Warrington 2-2—Etc 0- 3-1. Warrington: Boscow, back: Sampson, Jolley, and Speakman, three-quarter backs; Williams and Rowe, half backs: Molyneaux, Catterall, Bate, Russell, Barnes, Davies, Isherwood, Thornley, and Oxley, for- wards. Birkenhead: Jones, back; Norsworthy, Wat- son, and Kelly, three-quarter backs r. Hurst and Herbert halfbacks; Garner, Nelson, Sutherland, Morgan, Elliott, Atkinson, Tyas, Harper, and Jones, forwards. WARRINGTON v. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH.

This return match was played at Warrington on Satur- day in splendid football weather, and before a large attendance of spectators. In the first engagement this season Leeds gained a somewhat unexpected though. lucky victory, defeating the " wirepullers " by two goals to one goal, the former points being the result of a drop kick and a penalty kick. Since this match, however, the Leeds team have undergone several alterations, and, since their month's suspension have never thoroughly recovered. Several of their players have been sus- pended, but despite this they were able to place a good team in the field. Warrington were without their skipper and W. Dillon, the former reserving his energies for the gymnastic display which took place in the evening. About 4,000 spectators were present. Barnes met the kick off with a prompt reply to the half way flag, where Watson passed to Linton, play being contested at neutral territory. Short rushes by the Warrington forwards improved the homesters' position. Elliot here was at fault from a free kick taken by Frank Turner, and the Leeds goal narrowly escaped disaster. Massey made a grand effort to get in, but the tackling was safe. Watson, by the aid of a judicious run and kick, relieved the pressure, but it was only temporary, for a smart passing movement by Bate, Antrobus, Barnes, and Ladles& found the game once more near the pavilion goal. Lawless recovered some lost ground through a faulty pass, but a free kick to the Churchmen was neutra- lized by Barnes, who dodged and wriggled until he punted to Stewart, Massey meanwhile following up at a tremen- dous rate and preventing a reply. The home forwards were playing splendidly, each man displaying form which reflected the highest credit on him. A smart kick by Newton was well backed up by Oddy, who got away from a line-out, but his final pass was wide and the opportunity not taken. Nevins, Bandies, Turner, and Povey headed a dribble past ' the Leeds defence,' the ball finally gravitating in touch near the Leeds line. Watson cleared, only to find Barnes having a drop at goal, but the wind carried the ball wide of its mark, and only a minor, accrued. Bate dodged over from a line-out, but the point was not allowed, only a minor being awarded. This severe pres- sure could net last long without ,disaster to the Church- men, and succeeding Bate's effort at the corner flag a grand piece of passing between the same player and Barnes resulted in the home centre dodging over after a fine effort, the loud cheers which prevailed being re- newed when the same player converted the point. Barnes became prominent on the restart, meeting the kick off with a brilliant run and pass to Lawless, and the quarter flag was reached ere the movement was checked. Smart followingup by Donoghue, Nevins, and Evros prevented Stewart putting in a reply to a kick by Massey, who ran in surprising form, and after a grand effort succeeded in gaining the second try for his side. I Frank Turner failing at the difficult place. Evans was responsible for the reply to the kick off, and the visiting backs being at fault, the Leeds goal was again in jeop- ardy. The combined play of Warrington had its effect, and although Lawless had a try disallowed, amends were made immediately after, for another good pass to Massey gave this clever Warrington back another chance, which he quickly availed himself of, for after a zigzag run he placed the oval near the posts, Barnes again doing the needful with the place kick. The re-start found War- rington still on the attack, but they failed to make any addition to the score, which read at half-time as follows: —Warrington, 2-1-2; visitors, 0-0-0. Greenwood re- started, and the Tykes dribbling well Barnes appeared in a new role by a clever save. The Leeds men were severely pressed, and the game was only six minutes old when a passing bout between Bate and Antrobus resulted in the last-named running in with excellent judgment, enabling Barnes to place the third goal to his side's credit. A fine piece of play by Bandies, Nevins, Barnes, and Massey once more raised the siege, and Warrington taking advantage of the disorganized state of the visitors penned them in their quarters. Evansnarrowly escaped scoring, but Barnes receiving from Antrobus he ran and dodged, and cleverly eluding Stewart grounded near the posts,a fourth goal being registered from the place kick. Leeds now missed a grand chance of scoring immediately on the restart, and from a pack on the Warrington line Donohue and Frank Turner came away, and by accurate dribbling took play once more to the Parish 25. A neat sequence of passes between Bate, Antrobus, B,nd Barnes found play near the Leeds posts, and although Bate got clear away after Newton had cleared, his pass was a trifle forward and a grand chance of scoring was missed. Littlewood came in for notice with a dribble the length of the field, fatigue alone preventing a score. Faulty passing by the Warrington backs was the means of the visitors relieving, but exchange kicking between Nevins, Massey, and Elliott ended In the oval being scrimmaged near the Leeds quarter flag. Antrobus threw across to Barnes, who again dodged through the opposing backs, and grounded war the posts, the fifth gcal being registered. The visitors were a beaten team, and although they plodded en it was against hope, and towards the close of the match the play become a trifle loose. Chances of scoring were missed by Warrington,on one occasion fully half-a-dozen of the team failing to take the oval over ofter all opposition had been overcome. When the whistle sounded for "no side," the telegraph board showed the result to be as follows: Warrington, five goals, one try three minors; Leeds, nil. The game was remarkable for the fine combination shown by the Warringtonians, and to this must the vic- tory be attributed. There was not a weak spot in the team,and every department of the Rugby code was dis- played in a manner which reflected the greatest credit on them. Evans had very little to do but that was done well. Barnes was the hero of the match, and the fact of him scoring three tries and placing five goals out or five attempts at once shows that it was his day out Massey's play was sound and well finished, but Lawless has been, seen to better advantage. Both Antrobus and' Bate were in grand form, the latter for choice, but where all played so well in the forwards individual praise can. not be made. Teams :—Warrington : J. W. Evans, back; P. R. Lawless, T. Barnes, and J. Massey, three-quarter backs ;. W. Antrobus and J. T. Bate, half backs; Frank Turner, W. Nevins, T. Donohue,. Eyres, W. Bandies, J. Berry,. E. Dillon, R. Littlewood and W. , Povey, forwardS. Leeds Parish Church: A. Steward, back; J. Greenwood, J. Newton, and F. Elliott, three-quarter backs; W. Wat- son, and S. Swift, half backs; J. Oddy, T. Coop, R. Leech, H. Child, C. Clayton, H. Pickles, J. Davidson,. A.. Jackson, and C. Farrer, forwards. Referee : Mr. G-. W. Vickers, Salford. WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY LEAGUE. WARRINGTON V. ASPULL.

The first meeting of these clubs in connection with the above named competition took place on Mondayevening at Aspull, in brilliant weather. The Warringtonians failed to place their strongest team in the field, Barnes, Evans, Antrobus, Nevins, and Littlewood all being absentees. The honnsters were strongly represented, and at 5.30 Turner set the oval in motion on behalf of Aspull. Thorniley charging the kick off, a lucky recovery by Hulme taking play near the Warrington quarter flag. - loose passing hv the Warrington hark,: male

matters assume a serious aspect for the visitors, f and only the fine defensive play of Mather and Bate pre- vented the colliers from scoring. Passing by Bircball, Roberts and Morris found the lest-named running strongly, Massey pulling him up a yard from the line. Smart rushes by the_ visiting forwards and a kick by • Mather relieved, but another, bout at passing between the home backs almost ended in a tangible score, Pilk- , ington responded to a run and kick by Lawless, and from a scrimmage near the Warrington goal Hulme ob- tained posse,ssron and eluding Bate and Jolley, Bcecow tackled him, bat the homester managed to ground, the first try being recorded to Aspull, Turner. improving the point. This success of Aspull seemed to reuse the War- ringtonians, far on.tlhe restart the homesters were pen- ned inside their quarters. Mather got away, and Lawless was afforded a good chance of scoring, a knock on spo ing the opportunity From a line-out Fair Turner threw to Readies, who ran and passed to Lawless, and the last- named running well was eventually tackled, with the result that he passed the oval to his comparisons, and ; after another pretty exhibition bet Ween some half dozen players Mather made a dash across the line' scoring a brilliant try. Frank Turner, however, failed to increase the point. Bate and Mather showed up with neat pas- sing_ immediately on the re-start, and although Lawless made another good bid a moment later, the tackling of Morris prevented his travelling far. From a kick by Jolley, Hulme ran the oval out, but a neat piecs of work by Jolley again found the game at the Aspull end, and 'Pilkington was forced to concede a minor. The drop-out found the Aspull team making strong headway towards the Warrington goal, and good cross dribbling was well taken up by Hulme, who was tackled by Boscow, but the smart half back managed to ground near the corner flag. Turner was entrusted with the place kick, but failed. Frank Turner dropped out, and by the aid of a neat dribble, in which Donohue, Povey, W. Dillon, and Berry were the foremost Warrington invaded the Aspull half. The attack was staved off by Morris, who, with a judicious kick, made the visitors beat a retreat. A free kick to Aspull gained a little ground for Dillon and Randle@ with a combined dribble took the oval back to the half way flag where it remained at the call of half-time, the score then reading—Aspull, 1-1-0; Warrington, 0-1-1. The restart was followed by a long spell of give-and-take ' play, neutral ground being the scene of operations. Eventually Lawless put in a long kick, and Pilkington being at fault, Frank Turner raced up and although he mauled with the home custodian, and to all appearances succeeded in grounding, only a minor was awarded. This ill-luck did not deter the Warringtonians from keep- ing up the attack, and although Roberts came in for special notice with a lucky punt to Boscow, the Warring- ton custodian was safe, and a speedy return was the result. Jolley tricked Birchen, and a nice opening, was presented to the Warringtonians, but faulty picking up allowed the homesters to neutralize, and Aspull once more attacked. The fine play of Boscow was again of valuable aid. to his side, and his coolness and excellent judgment with his kicking were admirable. A tall kick by Hulme was brilliantly responded to, and a movement by Fair Turner, Bate, Jolley,- and E. ' Dillon + once more took play near the Aspull goal. Its stay here was but brief, for strong rushes and severe tackling of the visiting backs enabled the colliers to. clear, and a dribble by Welch took the leather over the line, a try being the result, Turner again failina at the place. Towards the close of the match Warrington pressed the Aspull men back on their lines, and although vigorous attempts were made to cross the borders, the colliers managed to keep their lines intact, and "No side "fixiud Aspull the victors by one goal and two tries, to Warrington one try and two minors. The play all through was vigorous and determined, and Aspull made the best use of the chances presented them, whilst Warrington failed in this respect on many occasions. Boscow, Bate, Randles, Frank Turner, Donohue, and Thorniley were the pick of the visitors. Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, back; Massey, T. .Tolley, and Lawless, three-quarters ; Bata and Mather half backs ;. Fair Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, W. Bandies, W. Povey, B. Berry, Thorniley, Donohue, and Frank Turner. Aspull Pilkington, back; • Roberts, Birchall, and Mbrris, three-quarters; Hulme and Cart- wright, half backs.; Turner, Donnelley, Webster, Taylor, Mather, Monks,.Lindsay, Acton, Smith. Referee, Mr. , Seddon, Broughton Rangers.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATT)RDAY, MARCH 22, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATT)RDAY, MARCH 22, 1890.
NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

_ To-day's matches :---Warrington v. Barrow, at Bar- row: Runcorn v. Liverpool 0 d Boys, at Runcorn Widnes v. Oldham,. at Whines; St. Helens v. Wigan, at St. Helens (League) ; St. Helens Recs. v. Leigh, at St. Helens.

Warrington put on a tall score on Saturday, when they sent such a prominent Yorkshire team as Leeds Parish Church back defeated by five goals, one try, and three minors to nothing. The wire-pullers were certainly seen at their best in every department. The forwards played with a vigour and dash that betokened victory, while every one• of the, backs displayed the highest form.

It has been said ,that this was Barnes' day out, and this is true, for "Temtatv " grounded no fewer than three tries, besides.placing all the five goals. The York- shiremen were, in, fact, completely bamboozled by the splendid dodging of the home three-quarter. But it was the half-backe "day out" too. Antrobus and Bate, as I have• before remarked, thoroughly understand each other, and'on Saturday they never failed in getting the ball clear, and their passing from each other and to the three-quarters was simply as accurate and well- timed as it could possibly be.

Philistine " otthe "'Athletic News," who gives a very readable descriptive account of the match,remarks "that the sturdy supporters a the Warringten club have still an overpowering confidence in the abilities of the team whenever they. meet any club not connected with the West Lancashire League, and, rather singular to relate, this confidence appears to be as contagious as a fever, for even the players seem to catch the infection, and, as a consequence, exhibit their true skill and scientific combination to thentter rout of the enemy. Why they are so low down ire the West Lancashire scale and so high up in other respects is a problem that can best be explained by themselves ; but the facts are there, and the determinationof Warrington to leave the competition very muck alone next season ought to give them the opportunity of improving the shining hour every week instead of at brilliant intervals. The match with Leeds Parish Church on Saturday, seemed to me to be a sort of consoling contest with brother miserables for competition don't appear to suit either team."

The picked "eight "of the Warrington Gymnasium Club are in good form iust now, and it is within the range of possibility that they may win the cup. Their success has passed all expectation, and it would not surprise me if, having got so far, they carry all before them. To dispose of three competing clubs, one of them ex,holders of the cup. is splendid work, and shoWs that they are in earnest. And, being in earnest, what may they not do ?, Their achievements are having a goad effect in the way of popularising the movement, and now that public attention has been so prominently. directed to the.usefulness of a good gymnasium, such an institution for Warrington is bound to become an accom- ' plished fact in the very :tear future. The way in which, the circus was. packed on the occasions of the two re-- cent competitions is striking evidence of the interest that is taken in the national contest.

div.head: MARQUIS, OF LORNE INTERVIEWS 'ITEE POPE.
div.p: MARQUIS, OF LORNE INTERVIEWS 'ITEE POPE.

A Rome telegram says the Marquis of Lorne, who re- cently arrived there from the south of France, was received in audience by the Pope, on Tuesday. The ceremony that obtainson the occasion of the reception of Royal and Princely personages was observed in connec- tion with the Marquis'g.visit to the Vatican, being desir- ous of emphasising the excellent relations existing with Great Britain, as the result of the mission of Sir J. Lintorn Simmons. The interview between the Marquis and the. Pope was marked by extreme cordiality, his Holiness expressing himself in sympathetic and compli- mentary terms in referring to England and its Govern- ment. The Princess Louise also was received by his Holiness, and the audience lasted half an hour.

div.head: NEW FRENCH MINISTRY.
div.p: THE NEW FRENCH MINISTRY.

Six ourof ten new French Ministers come from the South of France. Of the remaining four M. Yves-Gupt is a Breton, and was born at Dinan ; M. Bourgeois is a Parisian, while M. Devellb•is a native of Bar le Duc, and M. Ribot of the Department of the Pas de Calais. M. de Freycinet is the oldest member of the Cabinet, having first seen the light in 1828: The next in point of age is M. Barbey, born in 1831. M., Constans followed him closely in 1833. M. Jules Rteche and M. Fallieres both date from 1841 ; M. Bouvier from 1842. and M. Yves- Guyot fromthe following year. M. Develle was born in 1846, and M. Bourgeois,. the youngest member of the Cabinet, krlBsl. M. Bourgeois, by the way, would not be eligible for a seat in the Senate until next year, as candidates lor the Upper House must be forty years of age. •

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.

The strike of cut nailmakers in the Birmingham and Staffordshire districts terminated on Wednesday, the men having been granted an increase of 7i percent. The builders' labourers of Dublin, to the number of about BMOC', went out on strike on Wednesday for an ad- vance ()rid. an hour, the present pay being 3d. All building operations have consequently come to a stand- still.

div.head: STRIKE OF ENGINEERS.
div.p: STRIKE OF ENGINEERS.

The Press Association Newcastle-on-Tyne correspon- dent telegraphs that the strike.of engineers in the North of England, for the twelve o'clock Saturday became an accomplished fact on lVfbnday morning. The men directly affected number about 2Ocooo. Many more are involved.

div.head: LABOUR cO3g*RE'NCE IN BERLIN.
div.p: THE LABOUR cO3g*RE'NCE IN BERLIN.

_ The Conference on the Labour Question was opened in Berlin,,on Saturday. Baron von Boleosch, who was chosen president. said that the German Emperor was of opinion that the labour question demanded the attention of all civilized nations, owing to the dangers produced by industrial competition ;: and the object of the Confe- rence was to bring abont an agreement between the Governments of the States represented, in order that they might meet commontfangers by preventive measures. The clecision of the Conference would be subject to the,i approval of the Governments concerned, but the Presi- dent expressed the conviction that its labours would I exercise a beneficial itninence in Europe Secrecy is to ;be preserved regarding the proceedings of the Confeor once, which are to be conducted in French.
