- OUR NATIONAL POVERTY AND GOVERNMENT EXTRAVAGANCE. THE TREATMENT OF OUR BRAVE SOLDIERS. Sir,—Since I penned my last letter there died in the Workhouse, at Carmarthen, David Thomas, late of the 4th Light Dragoons, which regiment he joined in 1843. They lay at Carmarthen then and fought against "Rebecca and her Daughters " when that good lady and her children made an onslaught on the Workhouse there and endeavoured to pull it down. I knew some of the combatants on Rebecca's side. They made a brave stand did Rebecca and her daughters. Well, David Thomas enlisted and served as a soldier in various parts of the world for 26 years, served through the Crimean war, has the Crimea medal and four bars for Alma, Balaclava, Inkerman, and Sebastopol, the Turkish medal, and eight medals for distinguished service in the d after 28 years' distinguished service was discharged to hyber- nate on 9d. a day and to die in the Workhouse at Car- marthen—a town that boasts of a monumental column to Picton and a statue to Knott. Will you, sir, write his epitaph. recording his brave deeds, his long service, and be sure not to forget his pension of 9d. a day. It seems to be nobody's business to look after these poor men. Are there no good Samaritans? Are we all Priests and Levites who pass by on the other side without giving them even a look? Could not the Workhouse chaplains where these poor fellows are confined do some- thing to enlist the local public sympathy on their behalf? A circus proprietor at Rochdale gave them a benefit, and realised £3B, three weeks since. Can or will Warrington do anything in that way? Donoghue must be well-known in Warrington; he was the Miltia bandmaster for some 15 years after leaving the army, and trained several bands in the town, possibly ' more than a hundred men, some of whom under his tuition became good musicians,and who, if they knew his circumstances, would give a portion of their time and talent in getting up an entertainment for his benefit. He was discharged from the Militia thrmigh defective sight, not being able to see to read the music, and the loss of his teeth rendering him unable to lip the instrument. He now does a little at tailoring, but his sight is fast failing him, and his pension of Bd. a day will not go far towards keeping a home to- gether. Mu•t he, too die in the Workhouse ? After his discharge he had to go to the Workhouse for medical attendance in the endeavour to benefit his sight. It would be an indelible disgrace to Warrington and to Lancashire, with all its wealth, if this brave man should have again to enter the poorhouse to prevent being starved to death.. Fai!ing sight means loss of the means of living • a semi-blind tailor stands no chance of earning a livelihood. I don't think it would be very difficult to get up a fund that would give these poor fellows, who did and suffered so much at the call of duty, a small weekly allowance in addition to their wretched pittance of pension, that would make their in- come a pound or 255. a week. I expect it will be of no- use to ask the Government for anything; they will have us money for any one but placemen and royalty. Sup- posing some two or three, or half dozen, influential men moved earnestly in the matter—military men appealing to the benevolent public on behalf of their old com- panions in arms, would there be no generous response ? I think there would. Lord Cardigan told the remnant of the Six Hundred on their return from that ill-fated charge that their future would be provided for," No workhouse door will ever be opened for you. England will never suffer you to become paupers. How has that promise been kept? The men who relied upon its fulfilment have been sorely deceived. Can nothing be done to redeem that promise, even at this late hour? Do those elocutionists who take such pains to recite Tennyson's ode effectively, ever think or give a thought to those old men who sur- vive and took part in the exploit that prompted the poet to compose that ode. which they are so careful to give due expression to? They who rode into the jaws of death at the call of duty, expected nothing but thartheir last hour had come. To two-thirds of them Duty said DIE and they DIED. Don't let the survivors starve, if you can help it.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO.
Sankey Bridges, March 18, 1890.

"RITUALISM " IN THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND. Sir,—The prosecution of the Bishop of Lincoln is awakening the minds of the English people to the fact that there is a large and powerful body in the church who are endeavouring with all their powers to transform the Church of England, a church which is essentially Protestant and evangelical, into the condition, so far as doctrine is concerned, which obtained in the dark period previous to the great Reformation. In the first place, may be noted the increasing adop- tion of the Romish doctrine ot transubitantiation. It is a melancholy and alarming fact, that at the present time, this heretical and awful doctrine is openly preached in many of the churches in our land, the " Sacrifice " of the Mass for the quick and the dead being substituted for the Holy Communion, orLord's Supper ; in gorgeous and theatrical ritual taking the place of the solemn rite, which for centuries has been the usage of the Church ; the elemeuts being actually worshipped as God, and the officiating priest claiming the power to transform the bread and wine into the real and actual bodily pre- sence of Christ. From this awful doctrine the educated manhood of England recoils, rightly considering that a doctrine which is contrary to Scripture, contrary to common sense, and which is condemned in the very strongest terms by the Articles of the Church of England herself, and a doctrine on account of which that noble army (or "gang," as the Ritualists call them) of martyrs gave up their lifeblood, rather than acknowledge, must without any question be a grievously false doctrine. And, again must be noted the spirit of sacerdotalism which has of late arisen with such prominence in a cer- tain section of the Church. Many of the clergy now boldly preach the doctrine that the power given to the apostles to forgive sins, has by some miraculous means descended to them, and that at their own free will they are empowered to "retain the sins of whomsoever they will" ; in other words that if a person should die whose sins were thus " retained" by the priest he must neces- sarily go into perdition, and must be excluded from all participation in the benefits of the great atonement. This is a doctrine at which the manly mind of England must necessarily scoff and ..deride, AS being totally un- warranted by Scripture, and at the same time altogether opposed to common sense. The result of all these innovations is shown by the altered character of the attendance at those churches where these doctrines are preached. Instead of fathers of families attending regularly with their sons and families, men are now conspicuous by their absence. the bulk of the congregation, often a sparse one, being women and children. That this is recognised by those who practice these ceremonies, is proved by the follow- ing remarks made at a recent meeting of the principal Ritualist Society. "The stirring up of the Church, and the putting forth of higher spiritual claims, have had the deplorable effect of removing the bulk of the people from the Church. It is no use ignoring this fact, that to a minority the Church has become a thing of greater value, and higher meaning, yet to the bulk of the people the ordinances of the Church have become strange, and its principles unfamiliar." Not only are people leaving the Church, but how can it be expected that converts are to be gained amongst the hard-headed, rel-cting classes, men who look upon the bible, rather than the traditions of men, as the guide of their faith? How can it be expected that members of that ancient and noble race, the Jews, so many of whom are now so earnestly examining into the truth of the Christian religion, can be otherwise than repelled, if they should be brought into contact with expounders of such irrational and idolatrous doctrines? Is it to be wondered at that the Church is losing its hold upon the people, when the reflection is made, that those clergy? who could not have obtained their appoint- ments unless they professed their belief in the Articles of the Church of England, no sooner obtain those appoint- ments, than they preach and practice doctrines which are emphatically and specifically condemned by those Articles, which expressly state that they are "repugnant to the plain words of Scripture." Art. xxviii. If they believe in that dreadful doctrine of transubstantiation (if anyone can sincerely dose), let them have the honesty to go over to the Romish Church, but in the name of Common fairness, let them abstain from preaching Romisb superstition, and subverting the people from the Protestant fai,h, from the very pulpit of the Protestant church to which they professed adherence.

iiapily the country is Protestant to the core ; and there are indications that the people are beginning to feel that the time is approaching, when a determined and re- solute cessation of all this false doctrine and teaching must be insisted upon. For the same blood which ran in the veins of all that noble army of martyrs who were ruthlessly tortured and slaughtered by thepopish priests, still courses in the veins of the manhood of England; and if these encroachments upon our Protestantism by a pseudo-Romish priesthood do not cease, the manhood of England will again as heretofore raise throughout the length and breadth of the land an emphatic and peremp- tory cry of "No Popery."—Your obedient servant, A BANKER.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

THELWALL INSTITUTE. The Mechanics' Institute, in the hands of Mr. G. Manning, secretary, is a decided success. Tlae coffee rooms are very highly appreciated by many of the inhabitants of the district, and others from a distance who have visited them under the new management.
THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD. On Monday, an inquest was held by Mr. Yates, coroner, at the Ship Canal Hospital, Thelwall, relative to the death of the old man named Devon, who was killed at _
Latchford, on Friday, as reported in last week's "Exam- iner." Deceased was assisting at the bridge now in course of construction near Latchford Station, and whilst _ _

passing under a huge block of stone, weighing several tons, which was being raised into position on the bridge, the part of the stone near the" clip hole "gave way and the block descended on him, mutilating him in a shocking manner. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
THE MERSEY AND THE CANAL. REPORT BY ADMIRAL SIR G. H. RICHARDS. Admiral Sir G. T. Richards, acting conservator of the
Mersey, has issued his report for the year 1889, on the
state of the navigation of the river. Referring to the

progress made in the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal,Admiral Richards says that the straight train- ing bank or quay between Eastham ferry and the lock gates, measuring 900 yards is now completed. In con- nection with this part of the canal it may be mentioned that a powerful steam-hopper dredger, to be employed in deepening the entrance channel to the locks, will be com- pleted during the coming spring. The feundations of

the Eastham locks are in a forward state, and part of the side walls are constructed,. The locks have been length- 1 ened, in order to insert storm gates, on the recommenda- tion of Sir John Coode. The excavation of the canal over , B section, which extends a length of 1 mile 1,340 yards, , is in an advanced state, and the estuary embankment across Pool ,Hall bay is almost up to its full height. Although in an unfinished condition, this work did not suffer in any way from the heavy gale of the 17th October last. In section C, which measures 1 mile 40 yards, the deep rock-cutting is about two-thirds com- • pleted, the excavated stone being used for facing the estuary embankments. The cutting between Elles- mere Port Bay and the river Gowy is nearly completed. The large iron syphons for passing the tidal and other waters of the Gowy under the Ship Canal are now being constructed in a deep timber trench. The embankment on the section from the east side of Stanlow Point to Ince lighthouse is in a forward state. The cuttings from Ince light- house across the Frodsham Marsh to the west bank of the river Weaver are about two-thirds completed. They are entirely through marsh lands, along the whole length of which an outer embankment has been built. The con- crete wall between ,No Man's Land, at Runcorn and the Old Quay docks has been considerably added to since the last report. At the Old Quay docks the canal leaves the estuary and passes inland. The Randles Creek sluices, which are two miles above Old Quay Docks, have been completed during the past year; and from this point to Warrington the canal works are in a forward state, the greater part of the excavation being completed. The river diversion, or new cut, across the Arpley meadows at Warrington, is now completed, and the canal viaducts for the London and North-Western and Great Western Railways deviations near Warrington are also completed, and the foundations are in for the Mersey viaduct. Between Warrington and Manchester, a distance of about 15 miles, Admiral. Richards is infc.rmed, the canal works generally are in a forward state, and the locks at and above Latchford, the excavation of the Manchester and Salford docks, and the various embankments and viaducts for carrying the railways on the canal at a high level, are making satisfactory progress Admiral Richards also mentions that the embank- ment, of section D, across Port Ellesmere bay, has been commenced at each end and in the centre. In regard to this, we are informed that the aggregate length of the piles is no less than 70 miles, and that a great portion of them have now been put into position. heferring to section H, the Admiral states that the principal features of it are the works for discharging the tidal and other waters of the Weaver. These consist of ten sluices, 30ft. wide, and most of them were in position when the report was drawn up. Since then, we understand, the whole of the sluices have been completed. There is perhaps no portion of the Ship Canal works,Admiral Richards goes on to say, which is watched with more jealous supervision by those entrusted with the interests of the Mersey than those at the entrance of the Weaver. The river was originally of no navigable importance, but,by the aid of of engineering science it has become one of the most important non-tidal waterways in the kingdom. The general width of the river Weaver is about 100 ft. at the water level, and 45ft. at the bottom, and throughout the navigation there is now a depth of 10ft., which if neces- sary can be increased to 15ft. When the first portion of the Munchester Ship Canal is completed the Weaver vessels will be able to pass into it by a lock, specially constructed for the purpose at Weston Marsh, and will I then pass down the canal to Liverpool. this route being provided for them by the Canal Company, free of tolls. L It is doubtful, however, in the Adminilsopinion, whether any time will be saved in consequence, unless perhaps by the deeper-draught vessels, which cannot pass from the Weston locks directly into the Mersey on all tides.
DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD AND THE LATCHFORD BRIDGES.

Another meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board was held on Monday to consider the question of the bridges to be constructed over the Ship Canal at Latchford. Mr. Cliffe, the vice-chairman, pre- sided, and there was a moderate attendance of mem- bers. It may be explained that the agreement existing. between the Highway Board and the Ship Canal Company as to the Latchford bridges, is that there should be a swing bridge almost midway be- tween Grappenhall-lane and Knutsford-road, another swing bridge at Ackers-lane, and a high level footbridge to the high level station for Latchford that it is in- tended to construct. The Cheshire Country Council hav- ing objected to the removal of the swing bridge from a line with Knutsford-road, the Highway Board were now asked to agree to plans submitted by the Ship Canal Company, in which it was proposed in comply with the requirements of the County Council as to the swing bridge at Knutsford-road, and also to erect a high level vehicular bridge over the canal from Common-lane. Latchford, on condition that the Highway Board agreed to theabandonment of the swing bridge at Ackers-lane. Considerable conversation took place amongst the mem- bers of the Highway Board as to these new proposals. Mr. W. PIERPOINT remarked that he should like to know positively as to whether the new goods station at Latch- ford was to be on the high or low level. Mr. Parr said it was to be on the high level, but he (Mr. Pierpoint) maintained, upon what he considered good authority, that the station would be at the low level. If the station were to be at the high level there was, he could see, an absolute necessity for a high level bridge. In answer to Mr. JOHN DARBY. SHIRE, it was statea that the high level bridge would go under the new railway. Mr. DARRYSEIRS added that he hoped they would never sacrifice two swing bridges. He believed the railway company themselves would force the Ship Canal Company to construct the high level vehicular bridge. Mr. T. S. BURGESS Spoke strongly in favour of a high level bridge, and Mr. :PIERPOINT sug- gested that if a high level bridge was to be so great an advantage it shduli be made at Stockton Heath or to carry the Knutsford-read over the canal. Mr. J. C. PARR proposed that the plans involving a high level bridge in lieu of Acker's-lane bridge be accepted. Mr. S. DukotteS seconded. Mr. PIERPOINT and Mr. T. HALL opposed the proposal, and the CLERK (Mr. H. Linaker) remarked that if they passed that resolution they placed themselve en- tirely in the hands of the County Council and the Ship Canal Company. On being put to the vote, Mr. Parr's proposal was lost by eight votes to five. Mr. BURGESS then moved a resolution to the effect that the Board would agree to the abandonment of Ackers-lane budge on condition that the Ship Canal Company provide a high level bridge at Common-lane in lieu of the foot- bridge and make a road from there to Stockton Heath to end on the Northwich-road either near Twenty-step bridge, Mill-lane, or the Mulberry Tree Inn. Mr. J. C. PARR seconded the proposal. It was opposed by Mr. Pierpoint, Mr. John Darbyshirr and Mr. Ir. Hall, and the CLERK pointed out that it was in direct opposition t., the I one that had been already rejected. It was lost by six . votes to five. The meeting then terminated.

Local Agent, Mr. James Lewis, Chemist, Church-st., St. Helens.—Advt. A shocking murder was committed at Burton-on- rrent, on Thursday night. Frank Brierley, bricklayer, attacked a companion at his lodgings in Paget-st. with a razor, but his intended victim escaped and ran for the police. In the meantime, the landlord's daughter, Florence Barnes. aged four years, returned home from school, and Brierley attacked her, and nearly cut her head off. The pollee arrived and arrested him red-handed immediately after the crime, with the razor in his hand.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 22, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 22, 1890.
THE EFFEGT AT RUNCORN. Had the strike of colligrs continued the chemical worko

in Runcorn district would have been brought to a stand- still for want of fuel. On Wednesday about 300 men were stopped at the works of Wig,g Brothers and Steele, and about 100 men employed at tbe Runcorn and Weston works of the Alkali Company were thrown out of employ- ment. The coneilatory attitude of the mine owners will now set at rest the uneasy feeling that prevailed, ant work will be resumed as usual at the commencement of the week.

div.head: COAL TRADE CRISIS.
div.p: THE COAL TRADE CRISIS.
A COMPROMISE EFFECTED.
END OF THE STRIKE.
The conference arranged between coalowners and miners' delegates, which was proposed last Monday, had a successful termination on Thursday, an arai: . .
, cable agreement being arrived at. Both sides held private meetings at one o'clock on Thursday after- . .
noon, and the formal conference commencedat two

o'clock at the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, the proceedings thereat being kept private. The 'following were present on behalf of of the Coalowners, Federation :—Mr. J. D. Ellis, (South Yorkshire). Captain Harrison (Cannock Chase), Messrs. Alfred_ Hewlett (Lancashire), G.

Bond (Staveley), Watkin Davies '(Derbyshire), A. Barnes, M.P. (Lancashire), A. Chambers (Yorkshire), T. Drayton Grimke (Lancashire), F. N. Ellis (Leen Valley, Notts), Smallman (Warwickshire), W. E. Garforth (West Yorkshire), R. Hindsley (Lanca- shire), Fitzherbert Wright (Leicester), David Davy, Charles Ellis, Mark Oldroyd, .M.P„ CE., Parker Rhodes, and Thomas Carrington (South and West Yorkshire), with Messrs. Maskell Peace <ind F. Parker Rhodes, the secretaries. The men's

representatives were Messrs. B. Pickard, M.P., E. Cowey (Yorks), Samuel Woods, T. Aspin wall, and R. Isherwood (Lancashire), A. Longworth, James Haslam, W. E. Harvey (Derbyshire), W. Bailey (Notts), E. Edwards (North Stafford- shire), J. Stanley (Cannock Chase), B. Dean (Pelsall, South Staffordshire), J. H. Whitehouse (Somerset), and Thomas Ashton (Bradford, Manchester), secre-
tary. The proceedings lasted nearly three hours. At the conclusion of the meeting representatives of the press were informed that the following resolution
had been passed:— " That the men resume work, and that an advance

of 5 per cent, in wages be given now and a further advance of 5 per cent, in the first week in August." Arrangements for dealing with the wages question in future were agreed upon in principle. RECEPTION OF THE SETTLEMENT AT ST. HELENS. On Thursday all interest centred in the confer- ence at London, between the masters' and mens'

representatives. The prospects of a settlement were awaited with evident eagerness. Shortly after six o'clock in the evening, whilst a meeting of the St. Helens district Committee of the Miners Feder- ation was being held at the office of Mr. Glover, miners' agent, a telegram was received from Mr. Ashton, the Federation Secretary, which read as follows: " Settled ; 5 per cent. now, 5 in , August." The members of the Committee expressed their hearty satisfaction and agreement with the decision, which was quickly made known, and it spread rapidly throughout the town. On every hand it has been hailed with satisfaction. The strike in the coal trade has had a most serious effect on the trades of St. Helens and the immediatAlis- trict. In accordance with the decision of the miner's Federation last Friday week the whole of the colliers ' in the St. Helens district ceased work on Saturday, and when coming up the shafts they brought their tools in- eluding picks, spades, and lamps, with them. The col- liers affected, and all of which are included in the St. Helens district of the Miner's Federation, with the num- ber of miners who stopped work at each place, were as 'follows : Messrs. Pilkington Bros. (St. Helens collieries 1,100 ; White Cross Colliery Co., 600; Collins Green and Bold Collieries, 600 ; Ashton's Green Colliery (Messrs. Bromilow, Foster and Co.), 500; and the Pheenix Col- liery (Messrs. Glover, Urmson and Glover), 150. 1 Some thousands of men in the glass and chemical trades have either been completely stepped or put on short time during the week consequeat upon the scarcity of coal.

div.head: MASS MEETING AT ST. HELENS YESTERDAY.
div.p: MASS MEETING AT ST. HELENS YESTERDAY.

An open-air mass meeting of miners of St. Helens and district was held in Hardshaw fields near the Providence Hospital, St. Helens, yesterday afternoon. About 5,000 colliers attended and the proceedings were perfectly unanimous. Mr. Peter McKinley was elected to preside, and he was supported by Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent. Resolutions were unanimously passed accepting the terms agreed upon at the conference on Thursday, and expressing the hope that some means might be adopted whereby the wages of miners could be regulated accord- ing to the prices charged for coals. There will be a general resumption of work in the collieries of the district on Monday.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE STRIKE. WORKS STOPPED.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE STRIKE. WORKS STOPPED.

Some of the industries of Warrington have been during the week seriously affected by the great col- liers" strike, though the stoppage of works has not , been on so extensive a scale as in some neighbour- ing towns. At the Hallam and Bewsey works of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, there is a consumption of between 3,000 and 3,500 tons per week, and the deficiency in the supply was so quickly felt at at those large establishments, that between 1,500 and 2,000 of the employes ceased work on Saturday last, and have been idle all the week. In addition to these about 500 men engaged at the firms Wigan works and 2,000 at their colleries have been thrown out of work by the strike. At the Whitecross works all the linen usually employed at the iills have been idle since Monday, and also a large number of the wiredrawers, in all getting on towards a thousand men. Works has been very greatly impeded at the large establish- ment of Messrs. Monks Hall and Co., and at Sankey Wire Mills about 200 men ceased work on Thursday night. With regard to another branch of industry, the hands employed in the spinning department at Cockhedge Mills—about 500 in number—ceased work on Wednesday night, but a notice has already been posted at the works intimating that they will resume their employm-nt at the usual Moron Mon- 'day morning. Among the works which have had a sufficient supply of fuel to keep them going may be mentioned, Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Messrs. Rylands• Brothers, Longford Wire, Iron and steel , Company, Messrs. Robinson, Son, and Skinner, Messrs. Greening and Sons, and the Orford-lane Glassworks, &c. As might have been expected with so many men idle, the streets of the town have during the week borne quite a holiday appearance, so far as the groups of disengaged workmen were concerned. In most cases the enforced idleness seemed to be scarcely appreciated, and on Thursday evening and Friday morning, on its becoming known that the miners and their masters had come to terms, and that the strike was practically at an end, there was a general expression of satisfaction. THE GAS WORKS.

So far as the r-supply' of gas was concerned War- rington has not been injuriously affected by the strike, and on inquiry we learn that there was something like a fortnight's supply of coal in hind. In view, however, of possible emergencies the con- sumption of gas was economised to some extent by slightly limiting the supply to the larger, public lamps. The price of coke was raised at the gas- works to 15s. a ton.

• THE PRICE OF COAL. To local dealers in coal, who were fortunate enough to have a fair quantity in stock, it can hardly be said that the strike has been a misfortune. The retail price of the commodity may be said to have advanced during the week by "leaps and bounds," consumers in some cases having to pay as high as is. 3d. per cwt. In one case it is said, that a quantity was disposed of at the rate of Is. 6d. a cwt.' LYMM GAS WORKS. At a meeting of tl,e Lymm Local Board on Tuesday evening, the Law Clerk announced the receipt of letters from colliery owners at Atherton and Wigan, intimating that, owing to the miners having gone on strike, they would be unable to fulfil their contracts.—The Chairman explained that the colliery proprietors had a clause in the contract which enabled them to withdraw in the event of strikes. The Board had a supply of coal and cannel at the gas works sufficient to last two or three weeks, by the end of which time R was hoped that a settlement would have been arrived at by the miners and their masters.—Mr. Rogers observed that in view of the rise in the price of coal it would be advisable for the Board to raise the price of coke sold at the gas works Id. .Per cwt. Be moved that the price of coke be increased to 7d. per cwt.—The proposition was seconded by Mr. rhomason, and carried. WIDNES-3,900 MEN IDLE. The strike of colliers, as was anticipated, has had a very serious effect upon the staple trade of Widnes. When the trouble between the colliery proprietors and the miners commenced, the Widnes chemical manufac- turers gave their workmen notice that they would be unable to keep the works in operation in the event of a strike, and the men therefore viewed the course of events with great interest. Great regret was expressed when it became known that the miners had resolved upon a strike. Large numbers of chemical labourers were immediately thrown out of employment, and men were stopped daily at the various works. By Thursday night there would he between 3,000 and 4,000 men idle. In some of the works the only men employed are the tradesmen and finishers. The decision of the colliery proprietors to concede the advance to the colliers became widely known early yesterday morning, and was re- ceived with much joy because of putting an end to the strike. It is expected that the works will resume their ordinary routine at the beginning of the week, when fresh supplies of fuel can be obtained.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

The colliery village Oilfay—cio—ciis peculiarly affected by the strike. It is the centre of the wide coalfield covered by the well known firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and that firm provides the only means of livelihood for the entire population. The crisis in the staple industry has, therefore, excited no little interest among the villagers. Seven of the 15 pits owned by the firm of Messrs. Evans and Co., are situated in the township and not only the colliers are affected by the dispute, but their action has occasioned a complete cessation of labour at the surface. The whole of the miners stopped work on Saturday with the rest of the colliers in other districts, and up to Thursday no communications had passed between the masters and men in regard to the resuMption of work. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. .

Thoup.:h E—a—rie;t—o—w-n— and Newton have no collieries within their boundaries there are several pits on the out- skirts of the township,and many colliery-hands reside at Earlestown. The strike, however, has seriously affected a numbsr of the works in the district.

div.head: SHOCKING DOUBLE MURDER.
div.p: SHOCKING DOUBLE MURDER.

Thomas Argyle, a gardener, killed his wife and his grandchild, and then unsuccessfully attempted his own life, at Nottingham, on Monday. Argyle was seen in his garden bleeding from the head, and said he had killed his wife, who was found lying on the bed in their room with her throat cut. Their grandson was found in the next room similarly murdered. Argyle had tried to kill him- self with a poker. He will recover.
LORD R. CHURCHILL AND HIS CONSTITUENTS

Lord Randolph Churchill has written to the Chairman of the Paddington Conservative Association stat- ing that as the Council of the Association has wisely re- frained from expressing any opinion on his action, he thinks it unnecessary to resign. But he adds that, as political events develop, the special Commission will be designated in Tory circles by an adjective more common in popular use than is altogether agreeable to the polite ears of moralists and divines.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.

St. Patrick's Day was observed in London to an unusual extent on Monday by tne wearing of green rogettes, green ribbons, and sprays of shamrock. Drivers of omnibuses, cabs, and vans decorated their horses and whips with green favours.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

... The Warrington branch of the Irish National League, celebrated the day by holding the annual concert at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-et. It was attended by a large audience, and the excellent programme that was submitted was highly appreciated. The first item was a pianoforte selection by Mr. George Riley, after which Mr. Pat Beckebt (of Manchester) was encored for his singing of" Equal to Sandy," and Mrs. Sutton followed with "Barney 0 Hea." Mr. E. Whitehead contributed a humorous song, in character, entitled "There'll be good times in Ireland when the landlords go." Miss Matthews (of Liverpool) sang " Terence'S Farewell," she secured an encore, and sang in response "The Angel's Whisper." Mr. R. Campbell, Irish comedian, of Liverpool, created laughter by his humoroussong, en- titled • The Irish Carman." Miss Fanshaw was encored for her singing of " Rory 0 More," and replied with "Needles and Pins:: Mr. Dillon, who followed, sang "Father O'Flynn," and in response to a recall gave the "Kerry Dance." The second part of the programme comprised songs by Messrs. Dillon, Beckett, Campbell; Misses Fainhaw and Matthews, and Mrs. Sutton the concert terminating with" God save Ireland," Sutton, was played on the piano by Mr. Dillon. Mr. George Riley played the accompaniments.

div.head: MR. GLADS.CONE ADDRESSES THE AMERICANS BY PHONOGRAPH.
div.p: MR. GLADS.CONE ADDRESSES THE AMERICANS BY PHONOGRAPH.

On the 14th inst. by means of Edison's phonograph Mr. Gladstone addressed a meeting of many thousand members of the Mutual Building Association. The message was enthusiastically received, as not only was the voice of the great statesman reproduced, but the distinct periods of the breathing pauses were hen rd. _

This message was as follows. "10, St. James's-square, London. "The purpose of the meeting on the 14th, may I con- ceive, be summed up in two words, Self-Help and Thrift, and I cannot, although much occupied, refuse to send to it a few words of congratulation and good- will. "It is Self-help that makes the man, and man-making is the aim which the Almighty has everywhere impressed upon creation. It is Thrift by which Self-help for the masses dependent upon labour is principally made effective. For them, Thrift is the symbol and instrument of inde- pendence and of liberty; indispensable conditions of all permanent human good. " But Thrift is also the mother of Wealth; and here comes a danger into view. For Wealth is the mother of Temptation, and leads many of its possessors into a new form of slavery, more subtle and not less debasing than the old. From thisslavery may all lands, and especially all lands of the English tongue, hold themselves for ever free."

div.head: LIVERPOOL DOCK STRIKE.
div.p: LIVERPOOL DOCK STRIKE.
GIGANTIC PROCESSION,

Two thousand carters on Monday joined the Liverpod dock strikers, thereby intensifying the difficulty. A meeting of Liverpool magistrates was held on Mon- day afternoon to consider the position as to the strike, which had assumed much graver proportions. It was decided to bring to Liverpool a force of 500 military from Preston. An exciting scene took place at a masa meeting of strikers on the same afternoon, 15,000 men being present. A van loaded with grain passed and a number of men rushed at the cart, drove the carter away, pulled out the grain' and strewed it in the road. The secretary and others cal led to the men to stop, but their advice was unheeded. In the course of the fight the carter was seriously stabbed, and another man was knocked down and savagely kicked. Six mounted officers and 50 constables were soon on the spot. As the officers rode through the crowd they were received with showers of stones and bricks They, however, acted with great forbearance, and succeeded in dispersing the crowd. The dock labourers' strike has now extended to Birken- head, where all the men connected with the Union left work on Monday, and marched in a body through the town. On Monday the procession of the men on strike was larger than ever, it being estimated that between 20,000 and 30,000 men took part in it. On Monday night a strong detachment of Salford police arrived in Bootle for thi, purpose of assisting in the maintenance of order during the strike. Comfortable quarters have been provided for the men. Several mounted police were patrolling the borough at night, and everything was reported quiet. IMPORTED MEN. On Tuesday forenoon a number of imported men from various districts arrived at Lime-st. Station, and were immediately placed in omnibuses, on the top of which was a strong guard of police, the doors being also pro- tected by a number of plain clothes officers. Mr. Cuninghame Graham arrived in Liverpool on Tuesday, and addressed a mass meeting of strikers. Be- cause they were workmen, he said, the military were sent for. They might be killed, and no one cared. On Wednesday there was no apparent change of material importance in the history of the dock strike from the labourers' standpoint. Two leading mem- bers of the Employers' Labour Association, in the course of an interview with a Press representative, said so many imported men had presented themselves that many of them had to be sent back. Mr. M'Hugh, general secretary of the Dock Labottrers' Union, in addressing a Mass meeting at Bankhall on Wednesday, said there was no foundation for the statement that the coal-heavers had gone in again. The situation of the dock labourers was unchanged, and their powers of endurance were not a whit less than at the moment they first came out. Mr. M'Elueh road a resolution, passed by 4,000 dock laboer- ers in Glasgow, that work be not resumed on the Allan line vessels until the Liverpool strike was settled, or until Allan Brothers accepted unionrules. Mr. Cunning- ham-Graham, M.P., addressing the meeting after Mr. M'Hugh, said that what the men had to do was to be firm and have faith in their leaders. Mr. Tern Mann addressed the meeting to the same effect. Reports were current on Wednesday that a considerable number of union men bad seceded from the strike end *gone to work, but this statement has been proved difficult of absolute verification. ARRANGEMENTS FOR SETTLKVIENT. At the Liverpool dock- yesterday morning mattters were substantially without change. The correspondence between the Chamber of Com- merce and the Labourers: Union is in the same position as on Thursday. Inquiry yesterday shows that nos that the question of working with non-union men has been in effect given up by the union, there is a feeling, among shipowners in favour of meeting the men on the question of nightwork and meal hours in a spirit of con- ciliation.

The Prince of Wales on Monday afternoon held on be- half of the Queen the second levee of the season at St. James's Palace. It was what is known as collar day, all attending wearing their decorations. The assembly was thus more thau usually brilliant.
ALLEGED WIFE MURDER THROUGH JEALOUSY. _

An old man named William Whittlestone, aged sixty- seven, a labourer,living at Deepcar, near WS.ke/ield, was remanded by the magistrates at that place on Wednes- day charged with killing his wife. It was alleged that he was jealous of her, although she was sixty-four, and that on-Monday he so kicked and beat her that she died early on Wednesday morning.
EXIRA.ORDINARY SEQUEL TO THE INFLUENZA.

From Vienna comes the news that several cases of a new disease which originally appeared in Mantua after the subsidence of the recent influenza epidemic. and to which the people of that city gave the name of Na Nonna (Anglice, falling asleep,") have occurred in the comitat of Pressburg. PeOple suffering from the com- plaint fall into a death-like trance, lasting, four days, out of which the patient wakes in a state of intense exhaus- tion. Recovery is very slow,, but so far no fatal case leas been reported. All the patients who have been seized with Na Nonna had a most severe attack- of influenza during the winter.

div.head: CREWE MURDER.
div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.

THE JUDGE An THE CORONER. Richard and George Davies, charged with the Crewe murder, were removed from Knutsford Gaol to Chester Castle on Monday. A great crowd gathered at Chester. Justice Wills, in addressing the grand jury, said those assizes would long be remembered for certainly one of the most lamentable and extraordinary cases of murder that ever he remembered; but inasmuch as it appeared to him to be absolutely certain,it would be their duty to return a true bill, as it was invidence before him in the despositions that each of the accused liaisons had made a statement which, whether true or not, was most cogent evidence against himself, and each inculpated himself, directly charging himself as having shared in the con- coction and the completion of the murder. He thought the less he said about it the better. His lordship then referred at some length to the non-production of the coroner's depositions and the reason thereof. It will be remembered that at the inquest the coroner and jury required that the prisoners should be brought to the inn where the inquiry was held, and the police declined to take the men there. Certain evidence was then refused a hearing, the result being that an open verdict was returned. His Lordship said in substance the police acted rightly; there was no law which made it obligatory for the prisoners to be present or even represented at the inquest; and that the coroner in acting as he had done, had thrown on one side the privilege which he possessed of obtaining evidence as to facts which might not be otherwise brought forward.—The grand jury returned a true bill against Richard and George Davies. THURSDAY.—TRIAL OF THE PRISONERS. The trial of Richard and George Davies for the murder of their father, Richard Davies, a master tailor, of Crewe, was commenced at Chester Assizes, on Thursday, before Justice Wills. The case excited intense interest, and the court was densely packed. Mr. Roberts, who prosecuted, gave an outline of the facts. The deceased, Richard Davies, was a tailorand draper at aewe. He and some members of his family resided at Crewe, but he had also a house at The Hough, a village about three miles out of the ton, where his wife and some of his children lived. It was his cus- tom to spend Sunday there On Saturday night, the 25th January, the prisoner Richard Davies left the business house at Crewe, and walking home, arrived there about a quarter-past' ten o'clock. A little while afterwards the prisoner George Davies, who ' drove away from Crewe in a pony trap with the deceased, ran into the house and said his father had been stopped in the lane by two men. Richard ran out, and, other persons coming up, the dead body of the deceased was found tying in a pool of blood on the ground with a number of wounds upon the head. Inquiries were set on foot by the police, with the result that the- prisoners were taken in custody and charged with the murder. Whiler under arrest they both made written confessions, the effect of which was that the deceased had treated his wife and children with habitual cruelty, and that for that reason they had attacked and killed him with an axe, which was subsequently found ,near the scene of the murder. Emily Davies, daughter of the murdered man, was called. She stated that she lived at the Crewe shoo along with her father, the two prisoners also working there. Her evidence did not throw any fresh light on the crime, but in cross-examination by Mr. Malcolm Douglas, she stated that the deceased only allowed /3s for house- keeping expenses, both at the Crewe shop and the house at Hough where the rest of the family lived. Her father did not live with the others, of whom there were eight, but had better food. She added that the family had meat only on Sundays. Albert Edward Mozeley, manager of a shop continuous to that of the deceased, deposed to having on the night of the 20th January, shortly before the murder, heard the voice of the deceased calling to someone "Loose me : loose my throat." Mary Davies, wife of the deceased, described the circumstances under which she was apprised of the murder, and added that they had a few acres of land at Rough ,where they kept a cow, pigs, and poultry. Butter and eggs were sold, deceased receiving the proceeds, hut part of the produce was consumed in the house. The witness afterwards stated that deceased attended races as a bookmaker and was very violent towards her when he lost, striking her in the presence of her children point- ing guns at her, and lighting old newspapers under her tad for the purpose of hating it on fire. John Davies, a married son of the deceased, also gave evidence, after which police witnesses related what happened with refer- ence to the confessions of the prisoners, which have already been published. The trial was adjourned to next day.

VERDICT AND SENTENCE. The trial of Richard and George Davies was resumed at Chester Assizes yesterday, before Justice Wills. The assize hall was again crowded. Several members of the family of the murdered man were conducted to promin- ent seats, and were objects of painful interest. Evid- ence of the finding of the deceased's hat on the roadway at Hough was given. Mr. Roberts then addressed the jury for the Crown. He admitted deceased was not the man he should have been, either aa a husband or a father; but though this might '.ave been a motive, it was no excuse for the murder. The confes.sions of the prisoners were proofs against both of the accused. If the prisoners were acting with common consent, no matter which of them struck the blow, they were equally guilty.—Mr. Malcolm Douglas addressed the jury on behalf of the prisoner George, maintaining that there was nothing in his client's written statement to prove he had offered a single act of violence to his father.—Mr. Glascodine, on behalf of the prisoner Richard, after re- viewing the painful nature of th a circumstances, asked for a veraict of manslaughter. Mr. Justice Wills then summed up, pointing out that no family circumstances would justify the reduction of the crime from murder to manslaughter. The jury, having considered their verdict nronouneed the prisoners- " Guilty of wilful murder," but recommended them to mercy. The judge sentenced both prisoners to death in the usual manner.

div.head: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.

The usual quarterly meeting of the Wesleyan Society in Warrington was held in the vestry in- Bold-st., on Monday evening, tea being provided by the wives of the circuit stewards. After tea a meet ing was held, under the presidency of the superin- tent minister, the Rcv. John Gunnell. There were present, in addition to the Revs. W. Brooks and B. H. Jackson, circuit ministers, Messrs. R. H. Hensball, John Bennett, circuit stewards, R. Cook, W. Bennett, E. Richardson. Dr. Starkey Smith, W. Silcock, Councillor J. Shaw Green, and a large number of stewards, leaders, and local preachers. A long discussion took place upon the report of the numbers in the Chairman's statement of membership, which showed a slight diminution upon last year, and it was determined that an effort should be made to bring into membership many who now have some ' objection to joining the classes. The financial statement was read,and showed the finances of the circuit to be in a healthy condition. The Superintendent nominated Mr. J. Bennett, jun., of Bevrsey Hall, son of one of the circuit ' stewards, as a candidate for the ministry. Many of the members present spoke of the exceptional ability of Mr. John Bennett, the Chairman remarking that he had had the pleasure of nominating a great number of candidates, but he did not remember one who showed such unusual' capacity for the work of the ministry as Mr. Bennett, nor one whose heart seemed to be so thoroughly devoted' to the work. There was an ahsolute/y unanimous vote in favour of the candidate. A vote of thanks to the superintendent, the Rev. John Gurmell, for his services during the year, was unanimously passed, and he was requested to remain in the circuit for another year, which he consented to do. A formal invitation was then directed to be forwarded to Conference, asking that the Rev. A. Freeman should be mei:minted to Warrington circuit, to supply the:place of theßev. W. Brookes, who leaves Warrington at the end of the present connexiorxat rear. It was agreed to send a similar invitation to the Rev. Mr. Ta.sker tosupply the place of the Rev. E. H. Jackson, who also leaves at the end of the present con- nexional year. A formal consent was given to the trus7 tees of the Lymm Chapel, to enlarge and improve the schoolroom, and build vestries. A conversation took place with respect to the advisability of erecting a mission-room, or chapel in Battersby-lane‘ district,. and a special committee was appointed to, consider the matter.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT' TEACHE RS' ASSOCIATION. THE' DISPUTE AT ST. B'ARNABAS. The annual meeting Of this association was held in the old Music Hall, Market-place„ Warrington, on Saturday. The Secretary presented the- annual re- port, which stated that during the past year the nominal strength of the association increased con- siderably, but the numbers returned to the Execu- tive were not more than those of thepreceding year. Branches of the Benevolent Fund , and Provident Society of the N.U.T.,-with Miss Hossack and Miss E. Brookes as secretaries, have been formed, and a ' corresponding member, in the person of Mr. R. Y. Wool- lacott, appointed for the Orphanage Fund. It is fully anticipated that these very useful adjuncts to the National Union will flourish amongst us. In November last the sum of £9 Bs. 4d., arrears of salary due and wrongfully withheld was recovered for a member without recourse to legal proceedings. In January, two members of the association were forcibly ejected from their posts as head teachers, and appealed to the association for advice and assistance. It may not be out of place here to explain the action of the association and union in connection with this case. In December,,Mr. R. Y. Wooaactt and Miss M. E. Parsons, of St. Bs.rnabas School, received one month's notice each to terminate their engagements. They laid their case before the association, and it was strongly recommended to the Legal Defence Committee of the Union, who took up the matter at once. The teachers were, instructed to remain at their posts, and if forcibly ejected to have two reliable witnesses present. They were ejected ; andlVlessrs. Brimelow and Boelgins attended at the request of Mr. Woollacott as witnesses on his behalf, and not on behalf of the Associa- tion at all, as asserted by certain interested persons. The ejected teachers retained possession of alt the regis- ters, as advised, in order that when Proceeded against for their detention the legality of the ap- pointment of certain managers acting in opposition might be tested The result fully justified this action, for two of the so-called managers were declared by the judge not to be managers. This cleared the way for the prosecution by the Union for assault and wrongful dis- missal, which case comes on for trial in London ut June next. On the 22nd February, at a meeting of the Association, Mr. Woollacott and Miss Parsons were re- commended to the Etecutive for the Sustentation Fund and were at once placed upon it„pending the determin- ation of the legal proceedings in which they are con- cerned. The report of this meeting, which. appeared in one Warrington wetly, was very misleading, and cal- culated to do the Association injury. It is to be regretted that publicity should be given to any reports whatever springing from irresponsible persons. The libel case of Brown v. Short„which occupied so much of the attention of the Association last year, resulted a few days ago in a vekdiet for the plaintiff, who is a member of the Associ- ation, of £5 damages. The annual report having been approved and adopted, the polling for members of the executive of the N.U.T. was next proceeded with. The voting papers, having been duly completed, were sealed up at once and pOsted to the General Secretary. Five new members of the association were enrolled. The electkoi of officers of the association resulted in Mr. Jordon, St. Maryt, School, Buttermarket-st., being appointed' vice-president, Mr. flodgins, hon. secretary and treasurer, and Messrs. Brimelow, Singleton and Corney, and Misses Burrows and Finney as members of Committee. Mr. William Walltice„ Christ Church School, Latchford, becomes president of the association for the ensuing year. The annual Conference of the National Union will be held in London at Easter, to rhich Messrs. Wallace and Hodsins will proceed as representatives of the assoda- tion. After a vote of thanks to the new president fcß•his conduct in thechair, the meeting closed.

e' -VA, • -' 44,641 BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. SWINE FEVER. By THE BOARD OF AGRICULTURE. THE Board of Agriculture, by virtue and in exer- cise of the powers in them vested under The Board of Agriculture Act, 1889, and The Contagi,ous Diseases (Animals) Aets, 1878 to 1886, and of every other power enabling them in this behalf, do order, and it is hereby ordered, as follows :- 1. The following Area (namely),—in the Borough of War- rington, comprised within the following boundary, that is to say, from the centre d the bridge known as Bewsey Bridge in Bewsey Road, near to the offices of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, to the south side of the bridge carrying the Railway of the Cheshire Lines Committee over the said road at the northerly end thereof, thence in an easterly direction along such Railway to a point where such Railway crosses the Railway of the London and North- 'Western Railway Company, and thence in a southerly direc- tion along such last-mentioned Railway to Bewsey Bridge aforesaid, —which was declared by Order of the Board dated the thirtieth day of December, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-nine, to be an Area infected with swine-fever, is hereby declared to be free from swine-fever, and that Area shalt, as from the commencement of this Order, cease to be an Area infected with swine-fever. 2. This Order shall take effect from and immediately after the eighteenth day of March, ()air:thousand eight bundred and ninety. In witness whereof the Board of Agriculture have hereunto set their Official Seal this seventeenth day of March, one thousand eight hundred and ninety. (Signed.) G. A. LEACH, Secretary. WM. HY.. BROOK, Town Clerk. 19th March. 1890.

TWENTY THOUSAND ACRES AMERICAN PRO- PERTY FREE. In allotments of Farm, Fruit, and Vineyard Tracts of 40, 20. 10, and 5 acres each, and selected Residence or Business Lots. ONE of the above divisions of Real Estate Pro- perty, located either in the Golden State of fruitful California, or In the famous Orangegrove State of Florida, will be unconditionally given free from any charge for the land to any respectable person who sends his or her full name and post address to the American Office of the Californian and Southern Land Company at Cincinnati, Ohio, U.S.A. As soon as your name and address are received by the Com- pany, a free Land Warrant for one of the allotments of free property will be returned to you by first ocean post. The only, cost for the property will be an expense fee for executing a Warranty Transfer Title Deco in your favour, and having the signatures thereto legally acknowledged before the ploper officials. Such expense will in no case exceed 125., and is not to be paid until after you have received the Free Land War- -rant. When one or more members of the same family, or friends, wish to secure property together, the Company will issue to any applicant as many Free Lana Warrants as may be requested, not to exceed ten, to be given by the applicant to those whom he applies for. The object in making this extraordinary offer is to secure a diversified interest and ownership throughout the different countries of Europe in the lands owned and controlled by the above-named Company. When this is accomplished, the Company will open branch offices in various European Cities, and offer its large remaining properties for sale at a uniform price of LS per acre for Farm and Fruit Tracts, and £6 per Plot for Residence or Business Lots. It is believed by the Company that the diversified interest that will be thus secured by this preliminary method of advertising will amply compensate for the amount of pro- perty that is now offered FREE. If the number of names sent for free property is in excess of the amount of such property, those whose names are re- ceived first will secure it. Hence the advantage of sending name and address at once, • All that need be sent is an envelope bearing your name and post address ; this envelope to be enclosed in another, *and the outer envelope to be addressed as follows, THE CALIFORNIA AND SOUTHERN LAND CO., CINCINNATI, OHIO, U.S.A. NOTE.- -If preferred, application may be made to the Com- pany's Branch Office in London. A peony stamped self- addressed envelope sent to the Company's London Agent, Mr. W. H. FULLER, 8, College Chambers, High Holborn. Lon- don, will secure a FRED LAND WARRANT, issued by the Home Company, the same as if sent direct to the Head Office.

was much thought of the holiday. Mr. LEVESON-GOWER, the new member for-Stoke-On-Trent, took the oath and his seat. The House went into Committee of supply, and in answer to Captain VERNEY, Sir MicRAEL flscas- BEACH hoped that in the near future it would be possible to make some improvement in the Holyhead harbour. After questions had been asked with regard to the coin- age, Irish grievances were discussed, and Sir W. HAR- COURT severely criticised the Irish Secretary's methods and policy. The House adjourned at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock.

ENGLAND AND AFRICA. report has been received at Mozambique that Mr. John Buchanan, acting consul at Nyassa, has hoisted the Union Jack on the Shire River, the usual salute being afterwards fired in honour of the flag. Major Serpa Pinto has gone to Mossamedes, on the West Coast of Africa. THE MURDER OF MR. BENWELL. Burchell, the alleged murderer of the young English- man, Mr. Benwell, was conveyed from Niagara to Wood- stock Gaol, where he is to take his trial at the approach- ing assizes. While at the station a friend who was allowed to speak to him expressed a hope that he would be able to clear himself of the charge of murder. In a cheerful voice he replied, "There is not a doubt but I will. Good-bye, old fellow." ELECTION INTELLIGENCE. AYR. A large number of meetings were held in the division on Saturday night. Mr. Routledge, who spoke at Ayr, undertook to support the Eight Hours Bill. Mr. Sheehy, M.P., also spoke. THE EAST DOWN CONTEST. The Sheriff of County Down, on Thursday, received the writ for East Down, and fixed the nomination for Tuesday next, and the polling, if any, for the following Tuesday. LEICESTER. A letter has been received by the president of the , Leicester Gladstonian Liberal Association from Mr. A. M'Arthur, intimating that owing to delitate health, he will not stand for the borough at the next election. The hon. gentleman has represented the constituency for 16 years. THE SUPPOSED MURDER NEAR WIGAN. ARREST OF THE GIRL'S MOTHER. Ann Dickinson was on Saturday night arrested as an accessory to the murder of her daughter on the sth inst., at Ince, near Wigan, for which her husband is in custody. She was brought before the magistrates on Monday. The girl, whose body was found in a disused coalpit, was outraged as well as murdered. A police constable gave evidence that Mrs. Dickinson admitted when he was examining the house that when she returned home on the night her daughter was missing she found blood on the bedroom floor, and this she washed away. On this the woman was remanded, and will be brought up along with her husband. The arrest of the mother occasioned much excitement. POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS. The excitement in the Wigan district consequent upon the trigedy at Ince, on March 5, when a girl named Hannah Lydia Birchall, 8i years old, was outraged and her body thrown down a disused pit shaft, shows no sign of abatement. On Wednesday, William Dickinson, stepfather, and Ann Dickinson, mother of the victim, who are in custody on the charge of murder, were brought before Mr. W. J. Lamb, J.P., for the purpose of a remand, a disturbance, which at one time threatened to assume serious dimensions, occurred. An excitable mob, consisting chiefly of miners on strike, assembled in the vicinity of the county police buildings at Wigan, and as soon as the doors were opened, a rush was made for admittance. The space alloted to the general public was soonfilled, but, notwithstanding, the crowd still clam- oured for admission, and could not be held in check by the police in attendance. The doors of the court were forced open, and the police were overpowered. The proceedings in court were of short duration, and con- sisted of an application by Mr. Superintendent Brassing- ton for a remand until Tuesday, when the case for the prosecution will be conducted by Mr. T. R. Ellis, who has been retained by the Treasury. The court was, with some difficulty, cleared. Those present evidently expec- ted the case to be completed, and were of opinion that the magistrate and officials had retired in order to pre- vent any more persons seeking admission. After waiting for a few minutes the crowd quietly dispersed. THE INQUEST. The inquest on the body of the girl Birchall, found in a disused pit shaft at Ince, was on Thursday concluded at Wigan. A verdict was returned that the deceased was outraged and murdered by her step-father, William Dickenson, collier. Mr. Coroner Brighouse sgain dis- sented from Mr. Justice Wills in his direction that coroner's juries should receive hearsay evidence, even when person .5 are charged with murder or man- slaughter.
